#2648. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2645. NFL news, live updates: Jaguars WR Parker Washington out for Week 12 after suffering shoulder injury in practice; Colston Loveland to land on IR with knee injury

Week 12 of the NFL season kicked off with a rare Wednesday matchup between the Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams, prepping us for a full Thanksgiving feast that delivered fans a full helping of excitement (and then some). Bears-Lions, Eagles-Cowboys and Chiefs-Bills all came down to the wire, allowing no time for a post-Thanksgiving nap.

The Denver Broncos and Pittsburgh Steelers will face off Friday in a matchup that will have plenty of eyes drawn — even if not for reasons that are entirely due to the actual football being played on the field. Ahead of that matchup, the Steelers made headlines by reportedly benching veteran quarterback and former MVP Aaron Rodgers in favor of backup Mason Rudolph for Week 12 after recent struggles on offense.

This storyline then reached a fever pitch on Wednesday when Rodgers appeared on "The Pat McAfee Show" and went scorched-earth on a rant about head coach Mike McCarthy. Rodgers accused McCarthy of repeatedly falling asleep in meetings and ending a team breakdown with "1-2-3 Let's go Packers." Rodgers was released and officially cleared waivers, now free to sign with any team as a free agent.

We're watching plenty of injuries ahead of the action, including Las Vegas Raiders All-Pro tight end Brock Bowers, who missed Week 11 with an ankle injury, though he was reportedly pushing to play in that matchup. The Jacksonville Jaguars ruled out WR Parker Washington after he suffered a shoulder injury in practice this week, too, which will have fantasy managers looking for other options on the waiver wire.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more for Week 12.

There's reportedly more good news for Chicago Bears tight end Colston Loveland, who went down with a knee injury during a Thanksgiving win over the Detroit Lions.

Loveland is no longer expected to land on injured reserve after receiving a second opinion on his sprained MCL, per ESPN's Adam Schefter.

The Bears are considering Loveland "week-to-week."

So it's hard to say the loss on Thanksgiving this year was the worst the franchise has experienced. But it was bad. Really bad. Leading by 21 points against an Eagles team that lost Saquon Barkley early to injury, was on its third quarterback this season in Joe Milton III and had lost seven of eight, Dallas somehow couldn't close out the win. It was the biggest collapse by any team in a loss in NFL Thanksgiving history.

The worst part is it felt familiar. In Week 8 of this season the Cowboys had a similar failure, losing in overtime to a Cardinals team (now 3-8) after Arizona had benched its quarterback while trailing 24-10 in the fourth quarter.

"Pretty stunning," Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott told the media afterward. "I guess I said it a couple weeks ago after the Arizona game, how stunning that one was, but this definitely takes the cake."

The worst part might be that the Cowboys are again wasting a season of Prescott's prime. He is leading a tremendous offense and if he had more help he'd be getting NFL MVP consideration. But it's looking very unlikely he and the Cowboys will make the playoffs, at a hugely disappointing 5-7.

It seems hopeless going forward. Owner Jerry Jones and his staff need to make sure there's not a repeat in 2027. But how?

Adams is still a way's away from returning after needing surgery to repair a torn hamstring in late October. The timetable to return was 6-10 weeks and the wide receiver isn't returning any time soon.

Rams head coach Sean McVay said on Saturday that Adams' 21-day practice window will not be opened this week. "We're not there yet," he said, ruling out the wideout for a sixth consecutive game.

Behind the scenes, there was plenty of talking. James Palmer of NFL Network reported before the game that the team's leadership council — a group of veteran players who regularly meet with McCarthy — met on Wednesday and held an "airing of grievances" to address some of the stuff Rodgers was talking about. The meeting reportedly left McCarthy "humbled," but also allowed him to explain to the players why he handled everything the way he did.

The meeting apparently left the team on firmer footing, with Steelers cornerback Jalen Ramsey saying the team expressed its support to McCarthy:

"For the past couple days, we as players, we were like, 'Coach, you good.' Let us turn this up, let us get in our zone."

Quarterback Mason Rudolph, Rodgers' replacement under center, also said the players were behind McCarthy:

"I think the leadership council rallied around coach McCarthy. I think in a weird way, the adversity probably brought us closer together. We've just got to keep carrying that in week to week."

McCarthy, meanwhile, seemed happy with how the team responded:

"Everything that was discussed was healthy. Lot of things in there, but what came out of it was urgency. I thought our leaders did a tremendous job of bringing the urgency to their rooms and it definitely showed up."

With Kirk Cousins set as QB1, Kyler Murray will move into the backup role now that he is back from the hamstring injury that kept him out for three games.

Carson Wentz will now serve as the team's emergency backup.

"Kyler got some good work in today, took quite a bit of the reps this week," said Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell. "Feels pretty good. We'll assess him where he's at, but likely to be the backup. Carson would be the No. 3."

#2642. Observations after Sixers smoke Pacers, advance to NBA Cup quarterfinals

Observations after Sixers smoke Pacers, advance to NBA Cup quarterfinals originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers' NBA Cup hopes remain alive and well.

The team advanced to the Cup quarterfinals for the first time Friday night with a 111-87 road win over the Pacers that cemented their spot at the top of Eastern Conference Group B.

The Sixers moved to 16-4 overall and Indiana fell to 6-13.

The first Cup knockout game for the Sixers will be against the Hawks in Atlanta on Dec. 4 at 7 p.m. ET.

LeBron James posted 21 points, seven rebounds and six assists. Anfernee Simons scored 19 points off the bench.

Joel Embiid had 14 points and 11 rebounds. Tyrese Maxey added 14 points and six assists.

The Sixers were down Jaylen Brown (left hamstring injury management), Dean Wade (left hamstring injury management) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear).

The team told reporters in Indianapolis that Brown underwent an MRI which "showed no new injury." He did not travel on the Sixers' road trip, meaning he'll miss their game Saturday night in Houston against the Rockets.

Tyrese Haliburton (left hamstring strain) and T.J. McConnell (left hamstring injury management) were out for Indiana.

Here are observations on the Sixers' blowout win Friday night:

Dominick Barlow (12 points, eight rebounds) started for the first time in his fourth game of the season. Embiid returned after missing the last two games with an illness.

Barlow converted a lefty layup on the night's first possession. James sunk an early three-pointer from the left corner, then nailed another from the right. The Sixers held a double-digit lead when they turned to their bench.

Again, James recognized the Sixers would be best if he was aggressive early and fired away beyond the arc. And it certainly didn't hurt that he's been red-hot as a shooter lately. Over his last three games, James has gone 11 for 17 from three-point range (64.7 percent). He's scored at least 20 points in five straight.

James posted 11 points on 4-for-5 shooting in the first quarter. His lone miss was a heat-check three.

Maxey picked up his second foul with 6:47 left in the first quarter and Anfernee Simons subbed in.

The Sixers also added Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation and used 10 players in the first quarter. Simons knocked down a three with 6.8 seconds left in the first to give the team a 30-22 lead.

Maxey was scoreless until he made a floater near the midpoint of the second quarter. Outside of the foul trouble, he had a subpart start offensively. Maxey was a tad off as a jump shooter, began 1 for 7 from the floor, and couldn't find many chances to attack downhill. He committed three first-half turnovers, too.

The Sixers managed Maxey's rough patch just fine, in large part because the Pacers had a woeful shooting half. Indiana, which entered the game ranked 29th in the NBA with a 33.3 three-point percentage, went 2 for 17 in the first half. The Sixers played sturdy team defense and mixed in effective zone throughout the night.

The Sixers expanded their advantage to 27 points late in the third quarter with a flurry of three-pointers by Simons, who showed off his microwave scoring ability.

The team's lead stayed comfortable because Indiana's offense continued to pile up empty possessions. Pacers star Pascal Siakam missed 11 of his first 12 field goals.

The fourth quarter was drama-free and the Sixers reached the Cup quarterfinals thanks to their stingy defensive performance. Even with improved efficiency in garbage time, the Pacers finished at only 34.9 percent from the field and 13.5 percent from three-point range.

Before Friday night, the Sixers had held an opponent under 100 points once this season. They limited the Knicks to 93 in an Oct. 30 win that opened their Cup campaign.

#2635. Orlando Magic eliminated from NBA Cup, add 2 games to schedule

The Orlando Magic's run in the NBA Cup came to an end Friday night despite finishing group play with a 3-1 record.

Orlando was eliminated from the league's in-season tournament after failing to secure either a group title or the Eastern Conference wild-card berth.

Although Orlando joined Boston, Toronto and Miami with 3-1 records in NBA Cup play, point differential ultimately determined the wild-card winner.

Boston finished with a plus-67 point differential, ahead of Toronto (plus-34), Miami (plus-28) and Orlando (minus-1).

As a result of not advancing to the knockout stage, the NBA added two regular-season games to Orlando's schedule early Saturday morning.

The Magic will travel to Cleveland to face the Cavaliers on Dec. 6 at 6 p.m. at Rocket Arena.

Orlando will then return home to host the Chicago Bulls on Dec. 10 at 7 p.m. at Kia Center.

The team said tickets for the Bulls game went on sale Saturday and are available through the club's website and ticket office.

Both newly added games will be televised locally on MagicTV 27 and streamed on DAZN. They also will be broadcast on the Magic Audio Network.

The elimination ends Orlando's streak of advancing to the NBA Cup knockout rounds in each of the previous two seasons. The Magic reached the quarterfinals during the 2024-25 season and advanced to the semifinals last year, earning a trip to Las Vegas.

This year's NBA Cup knockout-round games will be played in NBA team markets, with the championship scheduled for historic Hinkle Fieldhouse in Indianapolis.

The NBA Cup debuted in 2023. The Los Angeles Lakers won the inaugural tournament, followed by the Milwaukee Bucks in 2024 and the New York Knicks in 2025.

For Orlando, the focus now shifts back to the regular season after falling just short of another NBA Cup appearance. The Magic will have to wait until next season for another opportunity to compete for the in-season tournament championship.

#2620. James can still take over ‘any given moment,' and Sixers trust he'll pick right spots

James can still take over 'any given moment,' and Sixers trust he'll pick right spots originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James isn't oblivious to the calendar and the clock.

He knows he'll turn 42 years old next month, he's ancient by NBA standards and decline is inevitable.

James also knows who he is and what he still can do, whatever the norms are for players of a certain age.

"I think his battle against Father Time is one of the most impressive things he's done over the course of his entire career," Heat head coach Erik Spoelstra said Wednesday before Miami's loss to the Sixers. "We all know and everybody always says that Father Time always wins. But right now he's giving Father Time hell."

James went on to record his first triple-double with the 15-4 Sixers, posting 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds. The four-time MVP is at 126 regular-season triple-doubles and counting in his career.

Only Russell Westbrook, Nikola Jokic, Oscar Robertson and Magic Johnson have more in NBA history. James is 17 above Philadelphia native and Sixers legend Wilt Chamberlain.

With Joel Embiid sidelined by illness for a second consecutive game and Jaylen Brown ruled out at halftime with left hamstring tightness, James' do-it-all performance was timely. Tyrese Maxey's 30-point, six-assist outing was essential, too.

"I'm just trying to play the game the right way," James said. "I don't think my job is to dominate the game every night for this ball club. We have a Finals MVP (Brown), we have a regular-season MVP (Embiid), we have an up-and-coming superstar at point guard, we've got a young fella in VJ (Edgecombe) who's up and coming as well.

"My dues are paid with what I've done. If they need me to dust off the cape from time to time, then I can still accomplish that. But that's not my job. … But if they need it, I can do it at any given moment."

James' night featured a flurry of very deep three-pointers in the second quarter.

He started the season 10 for 46 beyond the arc (21.7 percent), but his percentage has risen to 31.6 with two sweet-shooting games in a row.

"The work has been put in and I'm not ever worried about anything as far as my game," he said. "The difference between the start of the season and now is that my legs are feeling better, my ramp-up is feeling better.

"I'm about to be 42 years old in a month. S—, it takes a little bit longer for the ramp-up, but I've been feeling pretty good as of late. I don't ever second-guess myself … because I know the work that I put in."

While James' rebounding was perhaps the least spectacular aspect of his game, Sixers head coach Nick Nurse appreciated his work on the boards.

James has remained a statistically solid defensive rebounder into his 40s and he's one reason why the Sixers have made a major improvement in that department. According to Cleaning the Glass, the Sixers' opponents have grabbed 28.4 percent of their own misses, which ranks sixth in the NBA. The team ranked 27th last season.

Asked about James' cape comments, Maxey shouted out, "Dust it off then!" with a grin.

Maxey's not sure exactly when James will dramatically elevate his game, but he trusts the 22-time All-Star to pick the right spots.

"I don't know," Maxey said. "Early in the game, he was telling me he was tired. I said, 'Well, we don't have time for you to be tired.'

"But he does a good job of just managing the game. He knows when he needs to score, he knows when he needs to pass. We're going to need a lot from him. I know he's seasoned, but we expect a lot of him and he does that."

#2618. Mike McCarthy admits he hasn't spent enough time with the defense

After registering an unlikely 27-5 win over the previously 8-2 Broncos, Steelers coach Mike McCarthy wasn’t angry, resentful, or defiant.

He was the same guy he always is, and he admitted that (as former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers said this week), McCarthy hasn’t been sufficiently invested in the side of the ball that isn’t his personal expertise.

“I have not spent enough time with the defense,” McCarthy told reporters. “You know, and that’s something that, as far as job responsibility, job description, you know, these are things that’ll be looked at in the offseason. But, you know, it’s a point in our year where we’re making adjustments and definitely conscientious of it. But at the end of the day, we have to all do our jobs and make sure we’re giving the players the plan and all the other things that they need that we can perform and play with that type of urgency, physicality that we played today.”

McCarthy prefaced his comments with a lesson he learned as a boy, growing up in Pittsburgh.

“My father used to tell me all the time as a kid, ‘You tell the truth, you only have to tell your story once,’” McCarthy said.

The truth is that this week has entailed two sharply different versions of reality, where both things can indeed be the truth. One, McCarthy (like all of us) has flaws. Two, Rodgers should not have spoken about them publicly.

Rodgers clumsily defended his decision to break the code of a football locker room by texting this to Al Michaels: “The code or sanctity exists to protect the integrity of the locker room, not to provide immunity from accountability for its leadership.”

That’s fine, but how does disregarding the “sanctity” of the locker room (a word Rodgers undoubtedly selected in response to Tom Brady using it on Thursday) create “accountability”? McCarthy is accountable to team owner Art Rooney II. Not to the media or the fans.

And to what end? He was either doing it to help the Steelers save their season, or he was lashing out.

We’ll let you decide which explanation is more likely.

#2615. Arnold Palmer's longtime press secretary Doc Giffin dies at 98

LATROBE, Pa. (AP) — Donald "Doc" Giffin, who left his job as PGA Tour press secretary to become the personal assistant to Arnold Palmer for more than 50 years, died Saturday, his daughter said. He was 98.

Giffin worked briefly for United Press International before serving in the Korean War. He was a copy editor for the Pittsburgh Press when he took a job as press secretary for the tournament division of the PGA in 1962, as Palmer was in the midst of energizing the golf world.

Palmer hired him as his personal assistant in 1966. Giffin handled all of Palmer's affairs behind the scenes as a media liaison, speech writer and schedule keeper. He was at Palmer's side at Latrobe Country Club and at Bay Hill Lodge in Orlando, Florida, until Palmer died in September 2016.

Six months later, the press tent at Bay Hill for the Arnold Palmer Invitational was named "Doc Giffin Media Center."

"I'm thrilled — overwhelmed, really," Giffin said upon hearing the news in March 2017. "The media center has been my life, not only with Arnold but as press secretary for the tour before that and as a newspaper guy."

Palmer recalled watching the industrious Giffin during the 1962 playoff at the Masters, which Palmer won in a three-way playoff over Gary Player and Dow Finsterwald for his third green jacket.

"His job that Monday was to phone in the hole-by-hole action on the course to the crowded press room, where wire service reporters and writers sat poised on deadline," Palmer wrote in his autobiography, "A Golfer's Life."

It was four years later when Palmer spotted Griffin in the grill room at Florida Citrus Open, at a time when Palmer was getting overwhelmed by demands on his time.

"What I really needed was, in effect, a traveling secretary and somebody to run my home office, and Doc Giffin was the man I wanted to do it," Palmer wrote. "I count that as one of the wisest choices I ever made."

Giffin was a popular figure, not only as a conduit to Palmer but as a former newspaperman who built relationships over more than a half-century in golf. Even in Palmer's later years, Giffin would host media who came to Latrobe to see Palmer's massive shop where he worked on golf clubs, a lobby and office with framed letters on the walls from presidents and kings.

If Palmer was in town, Giffin would let him know so he could come down and greet them.

"Doc played an immense role in building the legend of Arnold Palmer," Alistair Johnston, former chairman of Arnold Palmer Enterprises, said in an interview with Kingdom magazine.

#2614. Rams guard Bill Murray out for season after torn Achilles in first career start

Rams guard Bill Murray got the first start of his NFL career on Wednesday against the Packers. It will also be his last game of the season.

Murray suffered a torn Achilles tendon in the game and will miss the rest of the season, according to Jeremy Fowler of ESPN.

The 29-year-old Murray had a long and difficult road to reach the point where he was starting in the NFL. He originally signed with the Patriots as an undrafted free agent defensive tackle out of William & Mary and spent three seasons on the practice squad. The Patriots liked his athletic profile and work ethic, and when he couldn’t crack the gameday lineup on defense, they moved him to the offensive line, but after three years and only one game played, they released him.

Murray then signed with the Bears, got on the field as a backup offensive lineman for three games in two years in Chicago, and was released again.

In 2025, Murray returned to the Patriots’ practice squad, got cut, then signed with the Colts’ practice squad, and got cut again.

At the start of training camp this year Murray signed with the Rams, and after the Rams lost offensive linemen Coleman Shelton and Dylan McMahon to injuries last week, Murray finally got his chance to start this week.

That lasted three quarters, and now Murray’s season is over.

#2612. Observations after James posts triple-double, Sixers beat Heat in NBA Cup

Observations after James posts triple-double, Sixers beat Heat in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James posted his first triple-double as a Sixer on Wednesday night and led his team to a 111-104 win over the Heat at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

James notched his 126th career regular-season triple-double with 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds for the 15-4 Sixers.

Tyrese Maxey scored 30 points and dished out six assists.

Giannis Antetokounmpo recorded 32 points and 14 rebounds for the 10-7 Heat.

The Sixers improved to 2-1 and Miami fell to 2-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup.

Jaylen Brown was ruled out at halftime with left hamstring tightness. He had six points on 2-for-8 shooting over 17 minutes.

"He'll get some imaging and we'll get the update tomorrow," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said.

Joel Embiid (illness) missed his second game in a row. The Sixers are set to visit the Pacers on Friday night in their final Cup group game.

"He's ill," Nurse said of Embiid. "I do not know whether he's going to Indiana yet or not. I guess we'll find that out late tomorrow afternoon."

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory over the Heat:

Nurse emphasized pregame that the Sixers needed an improved defensive performance.

"We've got to compete much better at the defensive end than we did Monday (against the Trail Blazers)," he said. "It's as simple as that."

The night did not begin in especially promising fashion on that front. Antetokounmpo powered through Brown and scored inside for the game's first bucket. His transition layup put Miami up 6-0. The Heat scored nine fast-break points in the first six minutes.

As he had Monday in the Sixers' loss to Portland, Jabari Walker started at center. He was among the Sixers who shared the daunting defensive assignment of Antetokounmpo.

Walker took a charge on the 10-time All-Star in the first quarter, but Antetounkmpo had a stellar start. He forcefully orchestrated Miami's offense, often plowing through the middle of the floor and finding efficient answers.

The Sixers' defense was better late in the first quarter and it didn't hurt when Antetokounmpo took a seat.

Maxey had an aggressive, productive first period, scoring 13 points. Dominick Barlow's tip-in gave the Sixers a 27-26 edge.

James drained three three-pointers early in the second quarter, including a confident, deep jumper that fired up a high-volume home crowd. He's shown that he remains capable of flipping a world-class switch and taking over games in a vast array of ways.

There's no question the 22-time All-Star is out of his early-season outside shooting slump. James has gone 8 for 11 from long range over his last two games. He's scored at least 20 points in four straight.

"I just play the game as it unfolds," James said. "I had a couple of opportunities and I was able to connect on them. I kind of know when my hand is feeling pretty good, especially from the outside. We'll see how long I can keep it going."

Adem Bona checked in early in the second quarter. He provided a string of excellent defensive possessions against Antetokounmpo, including an emphatic block and several well-guarded missed jumpers, although Bona did get called for three fouls in the second period.

Nurse was pleased with what he received defensively from both Bona (two blocks, six rebounds) and Barlow (nine points, eight rebounds) off the bench.

"They used their gifts," he said. "They're quick side to side, both of them. When they're in that kind of fighting mode like that … they did a good job. We tried to get Bona in there when Giannis was in, just for the rim protection. And Dom just played really, really (well) all over the place … on the defense, on the rebounding, on the running, on the cutting."

The Sixers played effective zone defense at the tail end of the second quarter and held a nine-point halftime lead. That grew as high as 16 points in the third quarter.

Miami pulled back within single digits, but the Sixers maintained a healthy advantage and James kept on making highlight plays. He lobbed the ball up to Edgecombe early in the fourth quarter and the second-year guard skied high to lay it in. James later connected with Barlow on an alley-oop.

Once the Sixers have a substantial lead, James' presence is a massive help offensively. He's very well-accustomed to conducting methodical half-court offense, identifying favorable matchups and turning to fruitful actions over and over. James will also still steam forward on the fast break when he sees the chance.

Maxey buried a step-back three to extend his team's lead to 111-95 with 2:29 on the clock and the Sixers polished off a professional win. The fans roared when James snatched the rebound required to reach his triple-double.

"We came out tonight with a different mentality, different energy," Maxey said. "Nurse got on us a little bit in the film (session) yesterday. He lit a fire for a lot of us, which is good. We needed it."

#2611. Tua Tagovailoa released by Falcons after 12 weeks, 1 appearance

Tua Tagovailoa's time with the Atlanta Falcons is over, the team announced on Saturday.

The two sides have agreed to part ways eight months after the 28-year-old quarterback signed a one-year, $1.215 million deal with the Falcons.

"Tua came to Atlanta to compete, and he conducted himself with character and graciousness throughout his time here," general manager Ian Cunningham said in a statement. "After thoughtful conversations with Tua's representatives, we felt this was the best path forward. We wish Tua and his family nothing but the best."

Tagovailoa will go on waivers Saturday, one day before the Falcons face the Minnesota Vikings. He will become a free agent if he goes unclaimed.

"Thank you to the Atlanta Falcons for allowing me to be a part of such a special organization," Tagovailoa wrote in a message on Instagram. "My family and I enjoyed our time here. I am grateful to Arthur Blank, Matt Ryan, Ian Cunningham, Kevin Stefanski, Tommy Rees, Alex Van Pelt, my teammates, trainers, staff and the fans for the opportunity. I'm forever thankful to have been a Falcon."

Tagovailoa was set to begin the season as the Falcons' QB1, but an oblique injury the week of the opener in September forced him out of the lineup and cost him the starting job. Cooper Rush started Atlanta's opening two games before making way for Michael Penix Jr.

It was in Week 5 during a 30-23 overtime loss to the Baltimore Ravens that Tagovailoa saw his only action of the season with the Falcons.

Coming in after Penix suffered a rib injury in the fourth quarter, Tagovailoa had one of his three pass attempts picked off by Kyle Hamilton to end the game.

Tagovailoa played the first six seasons of his NFL career with the Miami Dolphins after being the fifth overall pick in the 2020 draft. Though it was an up-and-down run with Miami, he did earn a Pro Bowl nod in 2023 after throwing for 4,624 yards and 29 touchdowns while leading the team to an 11-6 record and a playoff appearance.

#2610. Mason Rudolph: Aftermath of Aaron Rodgers on Pat McAfee was challenging for Steelers

Steelers quarterback Mason Rudolph said after beating the Broncos on Black Friday that the situation with Aaron Rodgers gave the team an additional challenge preparing for the game.

Asked about Rodgers, Rudolph answered carefully but made clear that he didn’t appreciate Rodgers going the Pat McAfee Show with a scorched-earth attack on coach Mike McCarthy.

“Very hard, very challenging,” Rudolph said. “On one hand, you’re thankful for the time you spent with him and everything you learned football-wise, and the friendship, but we obviously had a lot of stuff we had to filter through, and a lot of aftermath with his visit on national television. Unfortunate, but we turn the page.”

Rudolph said his teammates told him they were confident in him as their starting quarterback, which he appreciated.

“They all had the same mixed emotions that I did,” Rudolph said. “Like just shocked, what on earth just happened? When you wake up Wednesday morning. I thought that after the initial shock sort of passed through, they just made it known they were with me, behind me, and it wasn’t like a throw in the towel, season’s over vibe. . . . They had my back and I appreciate that.”

Rudolph also said his teammates are behind McCarthy, who did a great job leading the team in the aftermath of releasing Rodgers.

“It was impressive,” Rudolph said. “Neither of us had every been through that kind of week, plus you add in the short week. So I just can’t say enough. He’s obviously handling a multitude of managerial things and statements and press conferences, and then also taking the time to make sure that his playcalling responsibilities are first and foremost. I mean, unbelievable week. He balanced a lot. Proud of the way our team rallied around him and made it known, like, Dude we’re behind you. Let’s block out the noise and go win a game.”

The Steelers played perhaps their most impressive game of the season in Rudolph’s first start, and made a strong statement that they can win without Rodgers.

#2607. Milwaukee Bucks vs. Oklahoma City Thunder Preview & Game Thread: Back to basics?

Coming off two disappointing performances, the Milwaukee Bucks try to re-establish their scrappy persona against the Oklahoma City Thunder tonight in the second leg of their back-to-back. The Bucks showed they could battle teams like Portland and Philadelphia, playing five straight clutch-time games where they punched well above their weight class. However, that momentum has all but disappeared after two absolute clunkers against Brooklyn and Detroit. The Bucks will need to find a way to play competitive basketball against a Thunder team that is snake-bitten with injury and currently in the midst of a five-game losing streak. Yet again, the Bucks have a chance to win—will they take it?

Not to throw stones from a glass house, but the Thunder have been having a tough go. This has been an injury-plagued year for them, as they come into Milwaukee with seven players on the injury report. In just the third game of the year, the Thunder lost both Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren to injury; Williams suffered a fractured left fibula that will likely keep him out for the season, while Holmgren suffered a small patellar tendon tear that will keep him out for another 4-6 weeks. The Thunder started the year 3-0 but have since gone 7-9, and over the last two weeks, have played worse defence than the Bucks; per Cleaning the Glass, they allow 117.7 points per 100 possessions, while the Bucks have allowed 116.8.

Despite these setbacks, this is still the Thunder, and they still have Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, so nothing will come easy tonight. The Bucks are currently 23rd in turnovers per game (15.8), and the Thunder are the fifth-best team at scoring off of turnovers. Also, while the Thunder have struggled on defense overall, they are protecting the rim well, so the Bucks will need to create paint touches and spray out to shooters. The last two games have featured a lot of selfish basketball from just about everyone on the Bucks, a much different look than what they had shown previously. If the Bucks are going to get back on track, they will need their backcourt to lead the way, and after two pretty awful starts for Ryan Rollins, one must wonder whether he should remain a starter, with Brayden Burries looking like a more than suitable replacement.

No injury report yet because the Bucks are playing a back-to-back, but Kasparas Jakucionis is the one to watch.

The Bucks will need to rely on their frontcourt to help shift the balance, and with Chet Holmgren, Aday Mara, and Jaylin Williams all out, Kel'el Ware will have a real chance to make his presence felt on the boards. He will need to clean the glass on both ends, giving the Bucks extra attempts and closing out possessions.

Who: Milwaukee Bucks (2-18) vs. Oklahoma City Thunder (10-9).

Brayden Burries looks as hungry as ever and will keep the motor running after the loss in Detroit, posting his first 30-point game as a professional and leading the Bucks to an upset win!

#2605. 5 coaching mistakes in embarrassing loss vs. Eagles

The distaste surrounding the Dallas Cowboys couldn't be any worse. Once again, after having a big lead against a lesser opponent, the Cowboys unraveled at the end of the ballgame and lost. It's the second time this season the Cowboys have had a 98 percent win probability, only to squander it, resulting in a disappointing loss.

The Philadelphia Eagles were a dying bird lying in the middle of the road, and the Cowboys still couldn't put them out of their misery. No Dallas Goedert, no Saquon Barkley, Jordan Davis traded, and still, the Cowboys managed to blow the lead and fall to 5-7. It's unacceptable how poorly this team executes down the stretch of games. It's also unacceptable how the head coach does this week in and week out, only to promise that things will get better or that the problems will be fixed, yet the issues remain.

Dallas undoubtedly has a head coaching problem. When you reexamine many of the Cowboys' close losses this year, they can be tied back to a decision made by Brian Schottenheimer. That happened once again on Thanksgiving. Jerry Jones has stated that he will stand behind Schottenheimer, and that's a big mistake. Here are five coaching mistakes made during the game that cost the Cowboys.

Fourth quarter — 7:48 remaining | Dallas leads 38–30

As if the Cowboys hadn't made enough mistakes on special teams, Brian Schottenheimer decided to introduce another one. After Britain Covey returned a Bryan Anger punt 23 yards to the Dallas 49-yard line, Schottenheimer challenged the ruling regarding whether Covey was down by contact. The ruling stood, costing Dallas a timeout.

Considering what had transpired to this point in the game, why risk a timeout without compelling evidence that the ruling would be overturned? The Cowboys had already watched a 21-point lead shrink to eight, and Philadelphia was threatening to make things even more uncomfortable.

Fortunately, Cobie Durant intercepted Joe Milton three plays later, temporarily bailing out the Cowboys. Yet that doesn't necessarily absolve Schottenheimer of the decision. When you're watching a commanding lead evaporate, situational awareness becomes increasingly important. The failed challenge was another example of Dallas potentially making an already difficult situation more complicated than it needed to be.

In what was shaping up to be a tight race to the finish, timeouts were like gold, and Schottenheimer wasted a valuable resource. With that timeout, Dallas could have approached the end of the game with more flexibility.

Second half, particularly the fourth quarter | Dallas leads 31–10 late in the third quarter

There's a difference between running the clock and running an effective offense. Philadelphia had already lost Cooper DeJean, while CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens had demonstrated they could exploit the Eagles' secondary.

Still, Schottenheimer became increasingly conservative with his play selection, relying heavily on inside runs. Javonte Williams finished with 101 rushing yards on 29 carries, averaging just 3.5 yards per attempt. Meanwhile, Prescott averaged 10.4 yards per pass attempt. Which one do you think made more sense?

One particularly questionable sequence involved Jashaun Corbin being stopped on third-and-one early in the fourth quarter, preceding the blocked punt. Even in that scenario, you could still roll the dice on fourth down with your offense and try to maintain possession. It was surprising that by the fourth quarter, Dak Prescott hadn't hit the 300-yard passing mark, considering how well he was throwing the football. This was reminiscent of the Baltimore Ravens game earlier this year, when Schottenheimer elected to throttle back his scorching-hot offense to manage the clock.

In effect, Schottenheimer's decision to prioritize clock management over maintaining the offensive efficiency that helped Dallas establish its lead signaled the beginning of the end for the Cowboys. Dallas scored only 10 second-half points, and you can start to see why.

Nick Sorensen isn't in the clear either. Special teams breakdowns have cost the Cowboys multiple times this year, including the aforementioned game against the Ravens. Two special teams plays completely changed the complexion of the game.

Dallas probably should have gone for it on fourth down. Instead, the Cowboys chose not to. Dallas' opponents have been able to identify a weakness in its punt team and have come very close to blocking punts several times this season. Sorensen hasn't adjusted to this, and Ty Robinson was able to break through the protection and block Bryan Anger's punt. Kenny Moore II was all alone when he recovered the football and returned the blocked punt for a touchdown, cutting the Dallas lead to 31–24.

If you're trying to be conservative and merely escape with a win, it doesn't make much sense to kick the ball into the landing zone and give the Eagles a chance at a big return, but that's exactly what happened. Britain Covey found a big hole in the Cowboys' kickoff coverage and was free down the left sideline. Eventually, Caleb Downs and Brandon Aubrey chased Covey out of bounds.

However, the damage was done. Philadelphia started at the Dallas 42-yard line and scored three plays later with ease. Inadequate special teams preparation and a lack of operational discipline defined just how bad special teams were for the Cowboys yesterday.

Fourth quarter — 3:27 remaining | Dallas leads 38–30

Brandon Aubrey is not the same kicker he was a couple of years ago. As a long-distance kicker, his performance has declined tremendously. Look at his success rate from 50-plus yards by season to understand just how far that decline has gone.

This isn't a player worthy of taking the ball out of the offense's hands. He missed a 40-yard kick in a one-score game, preventing the team from extending its lead to 11 points. You can say the laces weren't out on the kick, but you still expect the highest-paid kicker to make that kick at that stage of the game.

For all the criticism surrounding the Dallas defense, it finally delivered the turnover the Cowboys desperately needed. The Cowboys had just forced Joe Milton into a rare mistake when he was intercepted by Cobie Durant, and once again, Schottenheimer took the conservative approach.

Dallas had a golden opportunity to secure another first down, drain more clock, and potentially finish the game with a touchdown. Instead, Schottenheimer's approach to the offensive plays preceding the field goal attempt was another example of what has become commonplace with Dallas: failing to execute down the stretch of games.

Fourth quarter — 0:55 remaining | Dallas leads 38–36

The coup de grâce. Going for it wasn't necessarily the wrong decision. Philadelphia was out of timeouts, and a first down would have effectively ended the game. The bigger problem was the play-call itself.

With Javonte Williams in the backfield and Prescott lined up under center, Dallas could have presented a more credible threat of the run. There's a debate to be had that maybe they should have run the ball in that situation.Instead, lining up in shotgun effectively told the Eagles to expect the pass, and there was no credible threat of the Cowboys electing to run the ball.

Schottenheimer called a drop-back pass looking for CeeDee Lamb on a slant. Philadelphia took away the primary option, and Prescott was sacked. The Eagles took over near midfield and needed only 11 yards to set up Jake Elliott's game-winning 59-yard field goal. The predictability of the play-calling played right into the Eagles' hands, and Jake Elliott made them pay.

If you're putting up great numbers and your team is in the top three, maybe four or five, maybe, but top three for sure, but top four or five you should still get some consideration, if your team is hovering in that area, and your numbers are off the charts, you should be hands down leading the conversation when it comes to Sixth Man of the Year. For me, he's a starter – with the way he's playing, he could start for somebody or he's Sixth Man of the Year. One of the two, because of the way he's playing, but more importantly, because of where we're sitting record-wise."

On the status of injured Deuce McBride, OG Anunoby and Jordan Clarkson:

"When they tell me they can play, they'll tell me."

On managing an unpredictable rotation amid injuries and occasionally losing track of players' minutes:

"The guys have been great, the guys that have been available. When their number is called they just go out there and try to play the best they can until somebody comes in and gets them. So from that standpoint it's been pretty easy, but it screws me up a little bit because I lose track of minutes. Sometimes this guy may play more minutes than I want or this guy may not play enough minutes. That has happened both ways. That's the only thing that it screws me up sometimes, you get lost with guys."

On how frustrating it was to miss a crucial free throw against Miami:

"It's frustrating, obviously, just the way we fought back and the poor decision-making I had in the fourth quarter and honestly throughout the game. I think that's the most frustrating part. We didn't get a chance to do stuff. Maybe big picture, but focusing on tonight, some of the things I did tonight were frustrating."

On whether the additional rest following NBA Cup elimination could benefit the Knicks:

"Whenever there is a chance to win something, you want to go win it. Regardless of whether there's a roller-coaster ride up or down, in the end it worked out [winning the title]. I think as a team we're going to figure out whatever still matters and whatever obstacle or hurdle we have. No matter what it is, we're going to figure it out."

On the mental and physical toll of repeatedly having to overcome significant deficits:

"Maybe a little bit mentally, but physically not that much. We should have been playing that way from the start. It's something that I think we're comfortable being able to fight back, but a position we don't want to be in."

On choosing Stephen Curry over Magic Johnson in an all-time point guard debate:

"I'm picking Steph Curry. I'm sorry. I got to have the person that you have to guard when he steps on the court, no matter where he is on the court. That threat, even just thinking, 'Oh, he might be open,' is scary for defenders. But then you have Magic Johnson who can make any pass and start any break. I prefer the shooting."

On Shamet's consistency and contributions on both ends of the floor:

"He's just brought it every game. Whatever is asked of him, he contributes on both sides of the ball. Obviously, he's playing defense at a high level, shooting the ball at a high level as well. Whatever is asked of him, he goes out there and does it."

On starting a Sixth Man of the Year campaign for Shamet:

"I would definitely like to start the hype around that."

On dealing with Miami's frontcourt of Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo:

"One guy has the second-most points in a game ever and the other guy, he's an MVP, a former MVP. It goes back to execution."

On failing to defend the NBA Cup title and looking forward to another championship run:

"Obviously disappointed we can't defend the Cup championship. But we still have a lot more games to get ourselves ready to defend the world championship."

On Shamet deserving to be the Sixth Man of the Year front-runner:

"He hasn't missed [a shot] since last year. I think he definitely should be in that conversation. I think he should be a front-runner. Obviously it's early in the year, but I think he should be a front-runner for that conversation. What he has brought to the team, in terms of obviously shot-making, taking on defensive assignments, those kinds of things, it has been at an extremely high level. Like I said, he should be the front-runner for that right now."

On what winning an NBA championship taught him about priorities:

"I don't really like occupying my time and my energy with that stuff. I think one thing last year, what winning a championship taught me, if you keep the right thing the main thing, a plethora of other things can come to fruition. I take a lot of pride in that. I just wanna keep the main thing the main thing. Whatever happens after that, is gravy."

On the Knicks' identity, defensive strength and ability to find ways to win close games:

"The Knicks, they know what their game is. They know how to win basketball games. Even if they're a little bit uneven at the start of the game or the start of the season, their defense has been really good and then they just figure out how to win games. Last year, I don't think they had the most unbelievable point differential, but if you got them in a close game, they would figure out how to get it done and that proved to be true in the playoffs and obviously in the Finals."

On Hart being one of the NBA's most unique players:

"Josh Hart is one of the most unique players in this league. I respect him because of his ability to impact winning and doing it in a totally different way than the modern way that young players come into this league — young players come into the league, they wanna be the No. 1 option and have the highest usage and that's when they'll impact the game the most, if they can play that way. He fills in all the intangibles that are not about that, but it impacts winning as much as anybody who has a super high usage."

"Well now he's got a huge championship ring on his hand. It's well-earned. He has the heart of a champion and I think he's had that for a long time. The one thing, we faced him in the playoffs a few years ago, and you feel him as a competitor. And that's probably the greatest compliment you could give him, is he's a world-class, top-percentile competitor.

"He transcends what his size may be and he's going to make you take note of him every single possession that he's out on the court. And in the moments of truth, that's probably when he showed up the biggest. I have respect for him as a competitor as much as I have for anyone in this league."

#2601. It's time for the clock to have tenths of a second

Football is a game of inches. And a game of seconds.

More accurately, it’s a game of margins. Small margins. Victory (and defeat) often resides in those margins.

That makes the rules regarding those margins even more important. And that’s why the operation of the clock in the final seconds of Thursday’s Chiefs-Bills game seemed to be so significant. Especially since it appeared that Kansas City’s final drive left four extra seconds for Buffalo to score the game-winning field goal. Which happened with the final snap showing four seconds on the clock.

The NFL pushed back on that perception on Friday, telling Mark Maske of Front Office Sports that there was no clock error. That the first-down shotgun snap muffed by quarterback Patrick Mahomes and recovered in a scrum by Mahomes with the whistle eventually blowing and Bills coach Joe Brady (as NBC’s Mike Tirico described it) “running down to take a timeout” justifiably resulted in the clock moving only one second.

The clock, as Tirico said after the play, showed 19 seconds. It appeared that the whistle blew with 22 seconds left. The clock ended up restoring the time to 25 seconds, after a play that began with 26 seconds on the clock. Which defies common sense and the general notion that the passage of time is objective.

(Maske didn’t address the second-down play, a five-yard run from tailback Emmett Johnson that had the whistle blow with 19 seconds left — before the clock magically jumped back to 20.)

Regardless of whether the vague and not-generally-known “officiating mechanics” somehow allow a snap, fumble, recovery, whistle, and a coach “running down to take a timeout” to justifiably consume only one second of clock time, precision matters in the moments approaching the expiration of the game. One way to achieve full precision would be to incorporate tenths of a second in the final minute of a quarter, like other time-based sports do.

As explained in the aftermath of the Michigan clock debacle that turned a Wolverines loss into a win on Labor Day weekend, the Eagles proposed adding tenths of a second twice in recent years, in 2023 and 2024. The effort failed because many of the existing clocks weren’t capable of showing tenths of seconds, and teams didn’t want to spend the money to adapt to the new rule.

It could return, we’re told. The league has in recent months (before the Michigan situation) begun taking a look at it again. The all-digital clocks apparently can now be reprogrammed to display tenths of a second without added expense.

A separate issue relates to tying the whistle to the clock, like the NBA does. That technology, we’re told, would be more difficult to deploy in a football stadium.

Making that whistle-clock connection even more challenging would be the “officiating mechanics” that allow a sequence that seemed to consume six seconds to be revised without extemporaneous explanation to take only one second.

Regardless, precision is important. Especially in the ongoing Wild West age of gambling. In a clock-based game, the clock should be respected with complete accuracy.

For now, between the clunky delay-of-game protocol (which gives the offense a little extra time to start the play but who knows how much?) and the idea that certain plays officially take less time than they actually did, pro football’s commitment to time seems to be less like basketball and more like soccer — where the game ends whenever the referee decides it has ended.

#2600. Topspiel thriller ends level as Frankfurt peg Stuttgart back twice

After taking over a quarter of an hour to really get going, Saturday's Topspiel between Stuttgart and Eintracht Frankfurt exploded into life, when Robin Koch saw red in the 19th minute.

This came less than three minutes after the first effort on target, when Jonathan Burkardt sent a bicycle kick comfortably towards the arms of Dennis Seimen, before the visitors were down to 10.

Or, as Stuttgart thought, when the Eintracht skipper caught striker Ermedin Demirovic, with no one between the pair and Noah Atubolu between the sticks. However, a subsequent VAR check and trip to the screen for Sascha Stegemann resulted in Koch staying on the pitch, much to the relief of the 6,000 visiting contingent housed near the incident.

From then on, Adi Hütter's side seized control, despite not being able to find the back of the net as Stuttgart struggled in the rather unorthodox 3-5-2 shape fielded by Sebastian Hoeneß.

Fares Chaibi, Burkardt, Younes Ebnoutailib, and more let rip to no avail, while Deniz Undav and Demirovic grew more isolated at the other end.

That would be the case until the 42nd minute, when VfB managed to get runners beyond the strike partnership for the first time on the night. And while it was perhaps more luck than judgement, local-boy Grischa Prömel was hardly going to turn down the chance to take on Atubolu, which he did calmly, whipping the ball around the onrushing goalkeeper.

However, perhaps offering some justice to Frankfurt, the lead would last just over five minutes, when a corner was bundled out to Ansgar Knauff, whose deflected effort looped over Seimen via captain Undav, resulting in the sides going into half-time level.

Hoeneß decided against changes at half-time, and normal service resumed, with the sizeable gap between the Stuttgart lines leaving Demirovic, in particular, on a hiding to nothing when it came to holding the ball for his teammates.

However, once again that didn't matter, with Die Schwaben taking the lead eight minutes into the second half through Luca Jaquez. Recycling the ball out wide after a corner, Undav clipped a teasing ball back to the edge of the six-yard box, and the Swiss defender rose highest and powered past Atubolu.

And almost identically to the first half, the visitors were level just over five minutes later, when Ebnoutailib hammered home from inside the box, after a lovely piece of play involving strike partner Burkardt - potentially handing another reality check to the hosts.

With 66 minutes on the clock, Hoeneß would look to the bench to make the much-needed changes, with Chris Führich and Bilal El Khannouss on in place of Atakan Karazor and Ramon Hendriks.

And within a matter of moments, Stuttgart looked a different side, with Führich in particular causing huge problems on the left.

The noise level continued to rise, and the match became end-to-end, as neither side seemed prepared to take just a point.

Tiago Tomas and Jamie Leweling combined well on the edge of the box with five to go, resulting in an effort fired wide, before Frankfurt won a free-kick in a tempting position at the other end.

Unfortunately, the memories of Omar Marmoush rattling in a set piece from that range two years ago remained just a memory for the travelling Eagles fans thanks to Jeff Chabot's block, but as had been the case since the substitutions, this was not a clash set to simply fizzle out.

However, the clock would beat both of them, with three minutes of added time coming to an end with the scores level at 2-2, keeping Frankfurt ahead of Stuttgart in the standings for the time being, while VfB may wonder what could have been had the needed changes been made earlier.

#2599. The Caleb Williams second contract looms, possibly sooner than anyone realizes

Football is business. It’s big business, and it’s getting bigger all the time.

For the league and the teams, it’s perfectly acceptable (in the eyes of the media and the fans) for them to treat football as the big business it is. When players do it, many bristle. The players, they’ll say, should be happy they’re being paid to play a game.

They have enough, why would they want more?

It’s a warped view of what the football business is. It’s for the league and the teams to maximize the revenue. It’s for the players to maximize their salaries.

And if it’s OK, for instance, for the league and the teams to push for 18 regular-season games or to peel Sunday contests away for more standalone weekday windows or to hopscotch the globe in an effort to make the sport an international powerhouse, a player should be allowed to be aggressive about his own financial position, too. He’s not being selfish; he’s being smart.

Enter Bears quarterback Caleb Williams. Even before he was drafted, Caleb and his father, Carl, were exploring business ideas for maximizing Caleb’s compensation. Carl, when speaking to agents, floated the idea of Caleb getting a slice of equity in the team that drafts him. (The NFL, at about the same time, changed the rules to seal off that possibility.) Caleb and Carl, as we’ve heard it, also considered creative concepts for minimizing the tax burden (like the owners always do), such as having Caleb’s wages paid into an LLC.

While none of their creative and potentially innovative concepts worked, there’s an obvious device hiding in plain sight. At Article 7, Section 3(k)(1) of the Collective Bargaining Agreement: “A Rookie Contract for a Drafted Rookie may not be renegotiated, amended or altered in any way until after the final regular season game of the player’s third contract year.”

The common belief is that a drafted player can get a second contract after his third season. The key term is “regular season.”

With Caleb Williams in his third season and the Bears at 9-2, there undoubtedly will be a postseason after his third regular season. Why shouldn’t he — and why wouldn’t he — want his second contract to be finalized in the window between the end of the 2026 regular season and the start of the 2026 postseason?

Beyond the fact that he has earned much more than he has been paid (thanks to a rookie wage scale aimed at keeping first-round busts from absconding with wealth they’ll never earn), Williams continues to carry the injury risk. The second contract shifts the injury risk to the team. He should want that transfer of risk to happen as soon as possible.

The problem is leverage. Williams isn’t going to refuse to play in the playoffs, even if he simply cites an “injury” to justify sitting out until he gets his contract. He’s all about the team, and that concept becomes even more important in the aftermath of Aaron Rodgers’s ultimate anti-team move from only three days ago.

Here’s what Caleb can do. He can send a very simple and direct message, if he’s willing to say it — and if he’s willing to follow through on it. He can tell the Bears, “Extend my contract before the first playoff game to a market-level deal or I will not sign a second contract until I become an unrestricted free agent.”

It won’t be easy, because the system is rigged against the players. Williams would have to finish his four-year rookie deal, his fifth-year option, and at least two (if not three) franchise tags before forcing his way to the open market. That’s up to eight seasons without getting the second contract he has earned.

That said, if any player can pull it off, it’s a quarterback. The risk of a career-altering injury (while not zero) is smaller than it is for the other positions. After his eighth NFL season (2031), Williams will have recently turned 30 — which is young relative to the other positions.

For the Bears, it would be prudent to get it done sooner than later. If Williams keeps performing like he has (and if he keeps improving), it’ll never get any cheaper than it will be after Week 18 of the 2026 regular season. The market will keep going up, and the salary cap will keep going up. Williams’s value, in turn, will keep going up.

It’s something to watch over the next six weeks. Even if the deal can’t be done until after Chicago’s Week 18 game at Minnesota concludes on January 9 or January 10, 2027, unofficial advance conversations can begin at any time.

All of this will surely make Bears fans nervous. But if the Bears are willing and able to become the first team to sign a draft pick in the window between the end of a player’s third regular season and the start of the playoffs, Williams’s future could be secured in Chicago for years to come.

And if Williams attempts to pursue this approach, no one should be upset. It’s strictly business. The same kind of business the league and the owners would conduct, if they were in that same position.

No rest for the weary as the Philadelphia 76ers close a back-to-back with a visit to the Houston Rockets on Saturday evening.

LeBron James continued his red hot shooting for another +20-point performance, Joel Embiid returned from illness to post a 14-point, 11-rebound double-double and Anfernee Simons hit five threes off the bench for a 19-point night.

Now, on to Saturday night against the Rockets.

The injury report is a bit of a mystery for this one right now as they are not due out until the early afternoon. We will keep you posted when they officially become available, but one can probably expect LeBron James and Joel Embiid to both be out for this one after they both played in last night's win. Jaylen Brown (hamstring) didn't make the trip, either.

The Rockets are pretty damn healthy for this one, with only Steven Adams on the report as questionable (knee).

Again, we'll let you know when we have more official information on the Sixers' availabilities.

Especially if James, Embiid and Brown are sidelined, this is going to be one of the more challenging games thus far for the Sixers. The Rockets are enjoying plenty of early-season success, much like the Sixers. They have won seven of their last nine and come into Saturday on a two-game win streak, and they have a lot going for them.

Alperen Sengun has been leading the way for the Rockets, with the center on an absolute tear to start the season. He is averaging 22.0 points, 9.3 rebounds and 7.2 assists per game and has already posted nine double-doubles and three triple-doubles in the Rockets' first 19 games. With Embiid likely sidelined, it's going to probably fall to Dominick Barlow and Jabari Walker to try to keep him contained Saturday night. Tough task.

Right up there with Sengun is Kevin Durant with the 38-year-old averaging 21.5 points per night. The Rockets have four other teammates averaging scoring in double-digits as a healthy team with a whole lot of depth.

The Rockets are one of the best shooting teams in the league, averaging 48.7% field goal shooting (NBA best) and 37.7% from long range (third in NBA) helping them to the highest offensive rating in the league (121.3). They are also one of the best offensive rebounding teams in the association right now, pulling in 13.9 per game (2nd in NBA). We all know how poorly the Sixers can rebound at times AND how they can get bombarded from long range, so this one could get ugly quick if Philadelphia isn't careful.

This is going to be a tough one with what we expect the injury report to look like. We will keep you posted as we know more officially who's in and who's out, but the Sixers are in for a challenge Saturday night regardless, even with all the talent at their disposal.

The Sixers and Rockets tip off at 8:30 p.m. ET.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

#2595. Bo Nix's stats continue to get worse in Year 3

When you draft a quarterback in the first round, you hope to see him improve over his first few years in the league. That is most certainly not what has happened for the Broncos with Bo Nix.

After Nix’s disastrous performance in the Broncos’ Black Friday loss against the Steelers, it’s fair to say that Nix is only getting worse. By just about any statistical measure you can look at, Nix is playing his worst football in Year 3.

Nix’s passer rating is a career-low 79.0, down from 87.8 in 2025 and 93.3 in 2024.

Nix’s yards-per-pass average is a career-low 5.9, down from 6.4 in 2025 and 6.7 in 2024.

Nix’s completion rate is a career-low 59.4 percent, down from 63.4 percent in 2025 and 66.3 percent in 2024.

Nix has thrown touchdowns on a career-low 3.3 percent of his passes, down from 4.1 percent in 2025 and 5.1 percent in 2024.

Nix is averaging a career-low 193.1 passing yards per game, down from 231.2 in 2025 and 222.1 in 2024.

Running the ball, Nix has become completely ineffective, averaging just 2.9 yards per carry after averaging 4.3 in 2025 and 4.7 in 2024. Nix’s rushing first downs have declined from 45 in 2024 to 25 in 2025 to just 12 this year.

Despite their quarterback taking a step backward, the Broncos are 8-3 and in first place in the AFC West. There’s every reason to believe Denver will be in the playoffs.

But the Broncos aren’t going to be able to do anything in the playoffs if Nix plays like he did against the Steelers. And the trends suggest Nix is only getting worse.

#2592. Doc Giffin, beloved Arnold Palmer assistant and golf fixture, dies at 98

Donald W. "Doc" Giffin, the longtime personal assistant and trusted aide to golf legend Arnold Palmer, died Nov. 28 at age 98, according to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette.

Giffin, who began his career in newspapers and later served as the traveling press secretary for the tournament division of the PGA of America, the precursor to the PGA Tour, spent more than 50 years as Palmer's right-hand man.

Born Nov. 18, 1928, in Crafton, Pennsylvania, Giffin earned the nickname "Doc" as a youngster because of his knack for tending to minor playground injuries. He graduated from the University of Pittsburgh in 1950, where he served as editor of The Pitt News, and briefly worked for United Press before being drafted into the Army during the Korean War. He was stationed at Fort Gordon in Augusta, Georgia.

After two years of military service, Giffin joined the now-defunct Pittsburgh Press, where he spent nine years, including seven in the sports department. In 1962, he became press secretary for the PGA's tournament division. Four years later, Palmer offered him a job that would define the rest of his professional life.

Giffin never forgot his first day working for Palmer. It came one day after golfer Tony Lema and his wife, Betty, were killed in a plane crash on July 24, 1966.

Over the next five decades, Giffin became far more than an assistant. He served as Palmer's gatekeeper, media liaison, speechwriter, scheduler, confidant and problem-solver.

More: Arnold Palmer would have been 97. The life and times of a golf legend

"Doc has done everything," Palmer, who died in 2016, once said. "He'd better not retire — I don't know what I'd do!"

The bond between the two men was recognized publicly in 2017, when the media center at the Arnold Palmer Invitational was renamed the Doc Giffin Media Center.

Because of his decades-long impact on the game, Giffin received numerous honors. The Western Pennsylvania Golf Association named him one of its 100 History Makers in 1999. He also received the Tri-State Section PGA Distinguished Service Award, was inducted into its Hall of Fame, earned the Metropolitan Golf Writers Association's Winnie Palmer Award in 2009 and received the Memorial Golf Journalism Award in 2015.

The USGA honored Giffin for his service to golf during the 2016 U.S. Open at Oakmont, 54 years after he covered Jack Nicklaus' playoff victory over hometown favorite Palmer as a newspaper reporter.

"Giffin was dressed up, as always, wearing his trademark tie," Golfweek's Jeff Babineau wrote that day. "They just don't make them like him anymore."

Adam Schupak is a senior writer for Golfweek, covering the PGA Tour.

This article originally appeared on Golfweek: Doc Giffin, beloved Arnold Palmer assistant and golf fixture, dies at 98

#2589. NBA Cup 2026 Update: Eight teams for knockout rounds set, including Spurs, 76ers, Celtics

Welcome to the knockout rounds of the NBA Cup.

Thirty teams have been narrowed down to eight for the single-elimination knockout rounds of the NBA Cup, which begin on Friday and Saturday. Here is a look at the bracket.

In the East, Detroit won Group A by beating Brooklyn (while sitting Cade Cunningham and Duncan Robinson); Philadelphia locked up Group B by crushing Indiana in a game where LeBron scored 20+ again to make Father Time continue to look foolish; and Atlanta won Group C with an 87-86 win against Boston but the Celtics still advance as the East Wild Card. The Hawks have been playing better than people realize, but this was also the kind of loss that reignites questions about the Celtics.

In the West, Dallas had clinched Group A before play on Friday but they beat Phoenix anyway; Memphis won Group B by beating Minnesota in a game where the Timberwolves were without LaMelo Ball and Anthony Edwards, but the Grizzlies were without Cameron Boozer; and Portland won Group C and the Spurs advanced as the Wildcard after beating the Lakers in a game that was a tale of two halves (and the Spurs dominated the second one, which is what mattered most).

From here on out, it's as straightforward as it gets: The eight teams that advance to the knockout round play a single-elimination tournament to reach the Cup Finals. The schedule for the first games is:

Philadelphia at Atlanta, 7 p.m. ET (Prime)San Antonio at Dallas, 9:30 p.m. ET (Prime)

Boston at Detroit, 7:30 p.m. ET (Prime)Memphis at Portland, 10 p.m. ET (Prime)

The final two teams left standing in the knockout round, one East and one West, will head to Indianapolis for the Dec. 11 championship game.

The teams that did not make the knockout round were given two games, one home and one away, against other teams that did not advance, bringing them to 82 games for the season. Those games will be played Sunday or Monday (Dec. 6 or 7), and on Dec. 10.

It's all about the money — players do not hide that it is the biggest motivation. Players talk openly about it. How much money? Here's the breakdown:

Player on championship team: $604,985Player on runner-up: $241,994Player on semifinals losing team: $120,997Player on quarterfinal losing team: $60,499

While even the championship money is comparable to another game check for a star like Victor Wembanyama or Jayson Tatum, it can be a meaningful bump for minimum-salary players on the end of the bench. The stars realize who they are playing for when things get serious.

The winning team gets a trophy, and teams will hang a banner.

The NBA is moving the NBA Cup Final to Indianapolis's iconic Hinkle Fieldhouse, the home of Butler University.

Famously, Hinkle Fieldhouse hosted the 1954 Indiana high school state championship game that inspired the 1986 movie "Hoosiers," and climactic scenes from the film were shot there.
