#2588. The Broncos have to get back on track in short order

The Denver Broncos endured a humbling loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers on Black Friday. It was a Murphy's Law gridiron affair for the Broncos. Moreover, a blown opportunity to make a run at the top seed in the AFC and better their position in the AFC West versus the Kansas City Chiefs.

With their road loss to the Steelers, the Broncos have now dropped to 8-3 on the season. However, they have a three-game trek in front of them against the Miami Dolphins, New York Jets, and Las Vegas Raiders—three teams who are really struggling this season.

In early December, they have to play their best ball of the season. The time is running out for excuses. They need to get back on track in short order and reel off a series of convincing wins to restore faith across Broncos Country. Most importantly, they need to do it for themselves.

A multi-game winning streak would give them a big confidence boost prior to their primetime showdown on Christmas versus the Buffalo Bills. Here are some thoughts on what the Broncos must do to get back to winning football games.

For the past few seasons, virtually every metric and analytic pegged Denver's offensive line as one of, if not the best unit in the National Football League. Sadly, this year's performance up front has signified a serious regression across the board at multiple positions. It's safe to say they no longer are one of the best front five in football.

That was exemplified in yesterday's matchup. The Steelers brought the heat early and often against the Broncos. Running a lot of Cover 1 looks and sending pressure, Denver's offensive lineman looked out of their element and had no answer for their ferocious front sevent.

Coinciding with this, I'm not keen on the idea of keeping a Ben Powers and Matt Peart rotation at left guard. How about just putting Alex Palczewski in and giving him reps to see if he can do better? The team extended him this offseason. Give the young player a chance to develop. What do you have to lose? It can't get much worse than the Powers-Peart combination.

Fans expecting a third-year leap from quarterback Bo Nix have to be disappointed in his performance this season. Sure, the issues up front in the trenches don't help matters. However, there is no doubting this year has been a big disappointment without the ascension and growth you want to see at the most important position in the game.

Whether it's completion percentage, touchdown output, or explosive plays—there has been a steep drop off compared to Nix's two first seasons. What's even more discouraging about that is Denver added more talent around him this offseason to help take his game to the next level. For the most part, those additions haven't paid off.

Outside of Pat Bryant, Denver's group of receivers looked extremely sluggish and had a lot of issues hanging onto the football against the Steelers. Prior to the season starting, I thought Courtland Sutton and Jaylen Waddle could potentially be one of the best duos in the league. So far, they've looked rather pedestrian and have underperformed. They have to be better down the stretch, or the Broncos won't have a shot at being a championship contender.

The offense has also lacked a lot of explosive plays. Last season, running back R.J. Harvey was a touchdown machine and provided Denver's offense with a great safety valve and explosive pass catcher out of the backfield. He is eligible to return this upcoming week for the Dolphins game if healthy. I think he can provide a spark the team has been missing recently in his absence. Hopefully, he can come back strong and show some of the explosiveness he did as a rookie.

There is no doubt the defense was put at an extreme disadvantage against the Steelers. Two of Nix's turnovers resulted in a fourteen-point swing for the opposition. It doesn't matter how good of a defense you are, that's extremely tough to overcome.

Even so, they have to be far more consistent down the stretch. Last season, we saw similar issues in the second half of the season. They weren't as good down the stretch as they were to start the year. Against the Steelers, their defensive trenches struggled to hold their own. Being able to stop the run and generate pressure will be key in the coming weeks.

Eyioma Uwazurike will be eligible to return for the New York Jets game in Week 14. It's quite evident they have missed him the past few contests and haven't been as strong up front without him in the lineup. Based on what I saw, rookie defensive lineman Tyler Onyedim isn't ready to take on a significant snap count.

On top of that, it was a rough performance for Patrick Surtain II. I'm confident he is going to bounce back. He is one of the best players in the NFL and has been a shutdown corner since entering the league six years ago. Surtain and the backend of the defense have an opportunity to shine over the next three games going up against Malik Willis, Geno Smith, and Fernando Mendoza. Hopefully, they can take advantage of that and make some big plays and force a few turnovers.

#2584. Final Five: Breaking down the clutch 113-109 Emirates Cup win over the Suns

The Dallas Mavericks grabbed an incredible 113-109 comeback win over the Phoenix Suns Friday night. The win came on the final day of Emirates Cup group play and gave the Mavs a 4-0 record in Cup games, good for the top seed in the knockout round. It also put the Mavs on a five game winning streak.

After a hot start, Dallas got cranked over most of the second and third quarters, trailing by as many as 21 points. A clutch game seemed highly unlikely, much less a win, but Mavs' fans got both after a furious comeback. The NBA defines the "clutch" as the final five minutes of a game when the score is within five or fewer points. Here we break down that exact scenario from the big Emirates Cup win.

The Mavericks entered the final five minutes of play with a large enough deficit that the game was not yet officially in the "clutch" category. Oso Ighodaro's dunk put the Suns up by eight points, but by this point, Dallas had already begun roaring back from the 17 point deficit they faced entering the final frame.

Zaccharie Risacher had a chance to gut the lead with the clock stopped, but spit his free throws, missing the first and hitting the second. The Suns missed a three-point attempt on the other end, which was a welcome sight after they shot better than 50% on high volume earlier in the game.

After the Phoenix missed three, the Mavs came back down court and Naji Marshall canned a three of his own to draw the Mavs within four points. Following the earlier Phoenix miss, the six-point swing was a big momentum shift. Phoenix tried to answer with another three, missed, got the rebound, then got blocked by Flagg.

Marshall struck again, draining another three-point shot to cut the deficit to a single point.

Phoenix had an immediate answer with a dunk on the other end by Ighodaro to give them a bit of breathing room. Christie then committed an offensive foul on the Mavericks' next possession, giving the ball back to Phoenix to potentially push to a two-possession game. By this point in the game, Dallas was locked in on defense and forced an over-and-back violation to regain possession of the ball.

Marshall capped off a personal eight-point scoring run with a hook shot to once again pull the Mavs to within a single point.

Phoenix once again answered the Mavs arrival right on the doorstep, when Collin Gillespie hit a 15-foot jumper.

The back-and-forth continued, this time with Flagg spelling Marshall's heater. Answering Gillespie's jumper with one of his own, Flagg pulled the Mavs back to within one point for the third time in just over a minute of game action. Dallas then got a stop on the other end.

Off a Christie rebound, Dallas went the other way and Flagg got to the rim. He missed a layup through contact that could have potentially been called a foul. Undeterred, he got his own rebound and put-back through contact that almost certainly should have garnered a whistle but didn't. Nonetheless, Dallas grabbed the lead with just under a minute remaining, forcing a Suns' timeout. Out of that timeout, Dallas got a stop.

Dallas was able to extend their one-possession lead to three points after Flagg hit a cold-blooded jumper from 14 feet out. The Suns subbed in Luke Kennard for his three-point shooting, but he didn't get the chance to put up a shot. Instead, Miles Bridges missed a three of his own. Christie soared for the rebound and was fouled before he landed, but there was no call. With two players draped on him, Christie stayed poised and eventually drew a foul. This was a huge sequence, because more than three second ran off the clock as a result of the initial no-call.

Christie calmly drained his well-earned free throws, all but applying a vice grip on the game with the two-possession margin.

Naji Marshall was denying Devin Booker from getting the ball on the Suns' inbound pass, but they eventually found their man. Marshall made an attempt to steal the inbound, which proved to be a valiant but miscalculated gamble. Tight to the sideline, Marshall lunged with no actual hope of getting a steal – had he gotten his hands on the ball he either would have tipped it out of bounds or carried out of bounds himself. Instead the pass got to Booker who hit a three-pointer with Marshall out of position. The Mavs called timeout to set things up.

With four seconds remaining, the Mavs inbounded to Christie who was immediately fouled. With a thinner margin than his previous trip, it was crucial for Christie to once again hit both of his attempts. Anything less that that would give the Suns a chance to tie or win. Christie was having none of it, and once again calmly swished both free throws. This left the Suns, who had no timeouts, with virtually no options. Marshall capped the game with a steal and Dallas completed a comeback from down 21 points.

In the clutch, Naji Marshall went on a personal eight-point scoring run. Prior to that, he had six points for the game. Flagg chased that with four-straight of his own. From there, it was Christie's turn. His free throw shooting iced the game in a situation where had he missed even one of his four attempts, things could have gotten much more tenuous. The rebound he pulled down to ear his first pair of free throws can't be understated either. He got himself in position and leaped probably about as high as he could. With two defenders on his back and plenty of contact, he came down with the board and maintained possession until a foul was called.

This was absolutely a game the Mavs could have lost in blowout fashion. A look at the third quarter scoreboard could make you think Dusty May was just moments away from waving the white flag. Instead, the Mavs stayed the course and started chipping away, then furiously whittled down the Suns' lead before finishing things off in the final minute. With the win, the Mavericks were a perfect 4-0 in Emirates Cup group play and take the top seed moving into the knockout stage.

#2580. Daniel Jones could land with Falcons, soon

Three big-name quarterbacks have been released in the past eight days. The first one out could be replacing the last one.

The Falcons have emerged as a candidate to sign Daniel Jones.

Abruptly cut by the Colts on November 20, most believed he’d consider joining a contender as a backup, or a member of the practice squad. As we hear it, he’s also contemplating the possibility of getting a head start with a potential suitor for 2027.

Other teams mentioned include the Cardinals and Jets.

Basically, a short-term stint to end the season becomes an audition. If all goes well, Jones re-signs after the season and potentially competes to be the starter next year.

In Atlanta, Michael Penix Jr. remains the starter. It’s possible, frankly, that the new regime in Atlanta (led by president of football Matt Ryan) has seen enough.

The biggest difference between the two general options is the ability to play. As a backup with a contender, he’d play only if the starter gets injured. As a member of a practice squad, he’d wait for a potential injury to a contender’s starter (and an invitation to replace him). As a fresh face for a failing team in 2026, he gets a chance to become part of the solution in 2027.

Stay tuned. Although we’re separately told that Jones has multiple options and has made no decisions, he could land with the Falcons as soon as Monday.

#2577. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2576. Falcons release QB Tua Tagovailoa 'after thoughtful conversations'

The Atlanta Falcons announced they released quarterback Tua Tagovailoa on Saturday, Nov. 28.

"Tua came to Atlanta to compete, and he conducted himself with character and graciousness throughout his time here," general manager Ian Cunningham said in a story posted to the team's official website. "After thoughtful conversations with Tua's representatives, we felt this was the best path forward. We wish Tua and his family nothing but the best."

Atlanta signed Tagovailoa to a one-year contract worth a veteran minimum of $1.215 million in the offseason, with the former Dolphins starter scheduled to make $54 million from his former team.

The money Atlanta paid Tagovailoa this season offset what Miami owed him. As such, it behooved Tagovailoa to take the veteran minimum deal, granting the Falcons maximum flexibility while ensuring the Dolphins remained on the hook for more than $50 million of his scheduled overall earnings for 2026.

Tagovailoa will now be subject to the NFL's waiver system. If he is not claimed by another team on waivers, he will be a free agent and can sign with any team.

Tagovailoa was named the Falcons starter during the preseason as Michael Penix Jr. continued to rehab from a torn ACL. However, Tagovailoa sustained an oblique injury in practice just before the season opener. He ultimately appeared in just one game, completing two passes in overtime against Baltimore on Oct. 11 before throwing an interception that sealed the victory for the Ravens.

Penix has started eight games for the Falcons (3-7) since returning from injury. He's completed 60.7% of his passes while accumulating 10 touchdowns and seven interceptions.

#2573. Packers Film Room: Love tosses 2 INTs

We looked at Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love's touchdown to Christian Watson earlier, but now we're digging into his two interceptions against the Rams.

The Rams are up 20-13 late in the 3rd quarter. Tyron Hopper has just picked off Matt Stafford, setting the Packers up with a 1st & 10 at the Rams' 43-yard line.

Their first play is a 5-yard run from Savion Williams. A successful run! Now facing 2nd & 5, they're taking a shot and looking to tie this sucker up.

They're in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) in 3×1 Nub formation (3 receivers to one side of the field, an in-line TE as the only receiver on the line on the opposite side). The Rams are showing a two-high safety look before the snap and they stay in that look post-snap (coming into this game, the Rams defense was ranked 23rd in post-snap safety rotation per SumerSports, so keeping the same look has been pretty standard for them this year).

The Packers are set up to attack that exact look. From the Trips side, Bo Melton [16] is running a deep Over route from the #3 spot, Matthew Golden [0] is running a vertical route from the #2 spot and Savion Williams [83] is running a deep in-cutting route behind Golden.

Love is initially looking to Melton on the Over, but the safety on the other side is driving down on that route. That tells Love that Golden is open in the middle. The split safety look means the Rams are in a MFO (Middle Field Open) defense, so Golden is supposed to cross the face of Jaylen McCollough [2] and work into that Open portion. With Melton tying up the other safety, this would give Golden inside leverage on McCullough and open space over the top.

Love does a nice job of bouncing in the pocket, then loading and throwing to Golden. As Love is starting his throwing motion, Golden drifts upfield, over the safety.

The ball goes to the middle, Golden is running the seam, and McCullough picks up an easy interception.

I took a screenshot not long after Love released this ball. You can clearly see the ball still in the air and Love throwing up his hands because he already knows this is going to be an interception.

It's the little things, and the little things are killing this team.

The Rams are now up 23-13, and I am asking the waitress for the check. The Packers are trying to claw their way back in this game, but the hour is getting late.

They are, once again, in 11 personnel in a 3×1 Nub look. In Trips Right, we've got Skyy Moore [23] at #3, Bo Melton [16] at #2 and Savion Williams [83] at #1.

The first read for Love on this is a version of a Smash concept between Melton and Williams. Melton is running a corner route over a pivot route from Williams. The read on this is Melton on the corner as the 1st read, Williams as the 2nd. Love would be reading Emmanuel Forbes [1] over Williams. Melton is uncovered at the snap and he has outside leverage on the safety (who is playing deep to take away any explosives). Even if someone underneath drops to Melton (which they do), Melton will still have outside leverage.

If Forbes stays on Williams underneath, Love will throw the corner to Melton. If Forbes bails to Melton, Love takes the throw to Williams. It's a standard high-low concept that has been around seemingly forever (reported to have been created by former Packers head coach Lindy Infante).

I say "Love would be reading Emmanuel Forbes," but he does not do that. Whether that's because he doesn't have time (Aaron Donald [99] wins quickly against Aaron Banks [65], not giving Love time to go elsewhere) or because he assumes Forbes is staying shallow, I don't know for sure (but I do have a theory I'll get to shortly).

Love checks Jaylen McCollough (the safety over Melton) at the snap and sees him retreating. He sets and fires to Melton. However, Love's assumption that Forbes is staying low is incorrect: after initially sticking with Williams, Forbes bails underneath the route from Melton.

Forbes comes down with a leaping interception and the game is effectively over.

Before we move to my next point, I want to take a look at Melton. He throws his hand up out of the break to signify that he is open. By the time the ball has arrived, Melton has cut his route short, giving Forbes an easy interception.

To be clear: this action doesn't influence the decision for Love to throw this. The ball is already on the way before Melton is out of his break. That being said, if you're confident enough to throw up your hand, you should be willing to finish the route and, in this case, at least make an attempt to knock the ball away.

Now, as to the assumption that Forbes would stay low. We saw a couple of examples of the Packers running similar concepts out of 3×1 looks. Early in the game, the Packers ran a Smash Fade concept. The boundary corner stayed low for that.

Later in the game, they ran Smash with Williams on the corner. The boundary corner stayed low for that.

Should Love still have confirmed Forbes was staying low? Yeah, I'd say so. Given what the Rams had shown to that point, I understand the assumption that he'd stay low, especially with the immediate pressure from Donald. The Rams set a trap and Love fell into it.

I'd still like to see Melton finish that route.

#2572. NBA Cup results finalize Phoenix’s remaining regular season schedule

NBA Cup group play has come to an end, and with the Phoenix Suns going 1-3 in the in-season tournament, we now know who their final two opponents will be to complete their 82-game schedule.

For those of you who aren't well-versed in NBA Cup scheduling, every team has been given an initial 80-game schedule since the tournament's inception in 2023. The final two games are determined by how teams perform in the NBA Cup. If you're one of the four teams in your conference that advances to the knockout rounds, your potential opponents are the other three teams that qualified. If you're fortunate enough to reach the NBA Cup Final, you get an 83rd game that doesn't count toward your regular season record. For the 22 teams that fail to advance, their remaining opponents are determined based on the results of group play and scheduling considerations.

So, based on the Suns going 1-3, what did they draw? Two teams that finished 2-2 in Cup play: the Houston Rockets and the Oklahoma City Thunder.

The Phoenix Suns weren't the worst team in the Western Conference as it pertains to NBA Cup group play. In fact, of the three teams that finished 1-3, Phoenix easily possessed the best point differential at -13. The New Orleans Pelicans and Los Angeles Clippers finished at -42 and -44, respectively.

Had the Suns taken care of business against the Dallas Mavericks on Friday night, they would've finished 2-2 and potentially had an opportunity to play one of the teams below them, including the Pelicans, Clippers, Jazz, or Kings. But alas, they'll be on the road in Houston on Sunday, December 6, before hosting the Oklahoma City Thunder on Thursday, December 10.

There is no perfect strategy for navigating NBA Cup play. I've held my tongue throughout much of the tournament because I didn't want to go on the same rant I seemingly go on every year. Now in its fourth season, I continue to find its existence neither particularly fun, nearly as colorful as the courts would have you believe, nor ultimately productive.

I love the idea of an in-season tournament, but I'm of the belief that none of these games should count toward your regular season record. Perhaps the league could reduce the regular season schedule to 72 games and introduce a more expansive tournament that brings the total number of games closer to 82. That way, they wouldn't lose any of that precious revenue we know they're struggling so desperately to obtain.

As it currently stands, the reward for winning is potentially tougher competition that counts against your regular season record. The reward for losing can also be tougher competition, albeit against teams that failed to advance to the knockout rounds.

The sweet spot? Be good in group play. Not too good. Look at the Denver Nuggets, who went 3-1 in group play and failed to advance to the knockout rounds. Their reward? Sacramento and Golden State.

If you're sitting around trying to figure out how to perfectly navigate a tournament so you can win basketball games without putting yourself in a position to face tougher competition down the road, what are we doing here? One game in the standings could ultimately determine whether or not you have home court advantage in the postseason. When a tournament creates a scenario in which there's a legitimate argument for being good enough to win games without being good enough to advance, I question the quality of the product.

Ultimately, I want the Suns to win basketball games without having to consider how those victories might adversely affect their schedule two weeks later. The NBA Cup should provide an additional incentive to compete, something that generates excitement without complicating the pursuit of postseason positioning. Until the league finds a way to separate those two objectives, I'll continue viewing the tournament as an unnecessarily complicated scheduling exercise with some obnoxiously painted basketball courts.

Clemson had one backer on ESPN's College GameDay ahead of Saturday's Palmetto Bowl. Kirk Herbstreit picked the Tigers to beat South Carolina at Memorial Stadium, pointing to an offense that has scored just 12 points over its last two games.

Herbstreit sided with Clemson despite a trend that favors the Gamecocks. The home team hasn't won in the series since 2018, and the Tigers have dropped the last two meetings in Death Valley. Still, after South Carolina managed just six points against Georgia last week, Herbstreit liked Clemson's chances to end that streak.

LaNorris Sellers was the reason two of his colleagues went the other way. Nick Saban picked South Carolina and said he expects the Gamecocks quarterback to make a statement on the road. Pat McAfee considered Clemson for his SuperDog pick, citing the home setting and what Dabo Swinney could draw on heading into the rivalry, but ultimately went with the Gamecocks because of Sellers.

Desmond Howard also picked South Carolina, as did celebrity guest picker Chris Paul, the former NBA All-Star and Wake Forest standout. That left Herbstreit as the only one of the five pickers to take Clemson.

The Tigers (7-4) enter the regular-season finale as 7.5-point underdogs, according to FanDuel Sportsbook. Clemson is coming off a 20-10 road win over Duke, while South Carolina (6-5) lost 34-6 to Georgia. Kickoff is set for 3 p.m. ET on ESPN2.

#2567. NFL predictions: Browns are ready for prime time against Raiders in what could be low-scoring game due to weather

This Sunday, the Cleveland Browns (6-4) take on the Las Vegas Raiders (4-7). Below, we analyze a few advantages, disadvantages, or general thoughts about the two teams before getting to our predictions for the game.

There have been a few games in which we've talked about the threat of rain, and it's either not turned out to be a factor, or has only impacted part of the game. However, the forecast right now for Sunday night's game is calling for darn-near guaranteed rain from start to finish. For that, we need to think back to Week 5, when the Browns lost to the New York Jets by a score of 17-12.

It was tough for either team to move the ball effectively, but the Browns got a couple big plays, including a 29-yard touchdown pass to take the lead mid-way through the fourth quarter. Then, the extra point was missed, presumably impacted by the weather.

On the next drive, the defense forced a fumble to take over at the Jets' 43 yard line. Cleveland went three-and-out, but a punt could still pin them back. The snap sailed over Corey Bojorquez, allowing the Jets to recover and then score a go-ahead touchdown on offense. That ended up holding for the Jets' win.

Every rainy game can be different. It's usually unlikely that you'll see a back-and-forth game of touchdown drives and efficient scoring drive. Without rain, I think I was optimistic that Cleveland could put together a dominant effort against Las Vegas. Now? It's just hard to predict. The weather becomes the X-factor, and you don't know which team it'll end up favoring.

Like I did last time there was bad weather projected, let's get into some of our miscellaneous notes this week that somewhat brushes the weather conditions aside for a second:

The key element for the Browns' offense this year has often been their passing game. And while I don't think this group will ever dominate a game from start-to-finish on the ground, or can be a run-first team, this is a game where the expectations for the rushing attack should be elevated.

The Raiders are 32nd in the NFL in run defense, allowing 149.5 yards per game and 4.82 yards per carry. In our five questions with our Las Vegas affiliate this week, they said that the team's defensive interior is the weakest spot on the team, and it's not even close. Cleveland should keep it simple and try running over the middle, neutralizing the pass rush that Maxx Crosby presents.

On the flip side, the Raiders feature the 32nd-ranked rushing attack in the NFL. That's a lot to try pairing on a rookie quarterback in Fernando Mendoza is the run game is putting them in third-and-long situations and Cleveland knows he'll be in passing situations against solid man coverage corners. In addition, tight end Brock Bowers, the team's top receiver, missed Friday's practice with an ankle injury and is questionable.

Cleveland might be without Denzel Boston, as he didn't practice all week with a quad injury. But Jerry Jeudy is ready to step up again, and I think Malachi Corley showed before the bye week that he's hungry for those opportunities as well if they come up.

According to FanDuel, the Browns are 4.5 point favorites against the Raiders. The over/under is 39.5.

Offensive coordinator Travis Switzer talked about the Raiders having difficulty stopping the run:

"I mean, certainly you might factor it in a little bit as far as some of the things you might want to do, but it ultimately comes down to us. No matter who they put out there, we got to execute our techniques in our place, and just trust those, no matter who's out there. So that's really, at the end of the day, it really comes down to focusing on us because that's what we can control anyway. And then as far as who they put out there, and we just talked, they're multiple schematically, too. So however they line up, we have to trust our rules, trust our techniques, and just go out there and execute. So that's really our focus."

Defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg was asked about Jared Verse having his best game of the season prior to the bye week:

"Yeah, it was great. It was great to see his energy. It was great to see the disruption he caused. It was great to see him celebrating with his teammates. And it's a reflection of the way he continues to prepare. Had a great week of practice prior to that, and he's off to a really good start this week."

Special teams coordinator Bryon Storer was asked about whether Raheim Sanders would go back to returning kicks if he's activated this week:

"Oh, absolutely. I mean, he has our longest kick return of the year and my belief is that you can never have enough quality kick returners on your roster. And to have Rocket back in the mix and being out there on the practice field, it makes me excited just to see him out there on the practice field and get him going. And he's definitely a better-than-average kick returner option. So, I would… it wouldn't be smart of me to not, you know, be excited and encouraged about the fact that maybe he has a chance to get back out there and return some kicks for us."

Here are predictions from multiple staff members at DBN:

Chris Pokorny: "Keep it simple, stupid. If the weather conditions are the way they are, I think Cleveland can lean on the run game, utilize some simple passes, and focus on ball security. With the Raiders, even though Mendoza had some success last week, I can see the weather conditions completely throwing off their ability to even move the ball. Jared Mueller: "Todd Monken won't let the Browns believe any hype coming out of the bye week. The Denzel Boston and Austin Barber injuries, on the other hand, are real concerns. The home crowd, and a slightly better start, gives Cleveland the win over Las Vegas." Browns 20, Raiders 17

Thomas Moore: "Have no idea what to expect or make of this Browns team. While it's cool they got flexed to Sunday night, this team can sometimes get full of its own headlines. Barry Shuck: "The Browns are a roller coaster. Yes, they are 6-4-0, but they haven't beaten anybody good. Well, the first Steelers game, but it appears now Pittsburgh is imploding. Curtiss Brown: "If you were to tell me that the Cleveland Browns would be playing meaningful games in November, you wouldn't believe me. But they are. The league chose to flex the Raiders-Browns game for a reason. Both teams are surprises considering how people viewed them before the season but the attention will be focused on 1st overall pick Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza.

For the Raiders, they aren't a bad team but they aren't particularly good. Offensively, the unit is one dimensional. Like the Browns, the Raiders can't run the ball at all but they are competent at pass blocking.

Defensively, an argument can be made that they are worse than last year despite the amount of money the unit invested. The unit young talent to be excited about but it's heavily flawed.

The last time the Browns played on Sunday Night football was 2021. Last time they had a home game on Sunday night? 2019. It's been a while. The city will be rocking and the team will be energized. Head coach Todd Monken has pretty much downplayed any hype surrounding the team and the Browns haven't played their best football yet. Will they? Not this week but this game could be closer than people think because the teams are somewhat similar.

Close game but the Raiders find a way to pull out a win but it wouldn't surprise if Cleveland won this game because Mendoza's debut will be in the cold with rain expected and that could be a factor. "

#2563. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

After the Lakers were knocked out of the NBA Cup, the previously unknown parts of their regular-season schedule were revealed on Friday night, featuring a first-time matchup and a familiar opponent.

The league announced the Lakers will travel to Oklahoma City to play the Thunder on Dec. 6 and host the Jazz on Dec. 10 for the two games added to their schedule.

The Lakers will get their first matchup against the Thunder since last season's playoffs. Getty Images

The Lakers were eliminated from the NBA Cup after Friday's road loss to the Spurs, with the Mavericks, Trail Blazers, Grizzlies and Thunder advancing to the Knockout Rounds from the Western Conference.

The Lakers-Thunder matchup will now be the first of four games between the teams, with previously scheduled games on Jan. 26 and March 6 in Los Angeles and April 1 in Oklahoma City.

The Thunder, led by reigning back-to-back MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, swept the Luka Doncic-less Lakers out of the playoffs in the second round in the spring to end their season before falling to the Spurs in seven games in the Western Conference finals.

They've been without Chet Holmgren, Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace since the trio sustained their respective injuries against the Clippers on Oct. 25.

The Lakers have a 2-1 series lead over the Jazz. AP Photo/Kyusung Gong

The matchup against the Jazz and Lakers will be the fourth and final regular-season meeting between the teams.

The game on Dec. 10 will be the third game in three weeks, with the Lakers falling to the Jazz on Nov. 18 to end their nine-game winning streak before beating the Jazz on Nov. 23, with both games being in Los Angeles.

The Lakers beat the Jazz on Oct. 25 in Salt Lake City for their third straight win to open the season.

#2557. NBA reviewing fan shoving Luka Doncic after Lakers-Spurs

SAN ANTONIO — The NBA will review the incident involving Luka Doncic and the fan after the Lakers' loss to the Spurs on Friday night at Frost Bank Center, a source told the California Post, which ultimately led to a male fan shoving the Lakers superstar.

The review is part of the league's standard process for these sorts of occurrences.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic #77 is shoved by a Spurs fan sitting courtside in San Antonio. Amazon Prime

Amazon Prime Video's broadcast showed Doncic tossing his white wristband into the first row of the stands postgame as he walked toward the visitors locker room.

The wristband landed at a woman as the Slovenian superstar continued walking toward the tunnel, with the woman appearing to say something to the Lakers superstar beforehand.

A couple of seconds later, Doncic doubled back to retrieve his wristband.

That's when things escalated, with the woman's male companion, who picked up the wristband, shoving the six-time All-Star with his right hand after handing the wristband to Doncic.

Los Angeles Lakers guard Luka Doncic is shoved by a Spurs fan sitting courtside in San Antonio.

"I just threw my wristband like I do almost every game, and then I heard she or he didn't want it," Doncic explained postgame. "So I went back to grab it, and he just pushed me, and then I gave it to somebody else."

Lakers forward Jarred Vanderbilt pulled Doncic back from the fans after the shove before leaning back toward them, with team and arena security immediately intervening.

Two-way big man Carson Cooper held Vanderbilt back as security motioned that the male fan was being ejected from the arena.

It wasn't clear whether the male fan also said something to Doncic before or after the shove.

Whether there would be punishments stemming from the incident was unknown as of Saturday morning, but the league will go through its standard review process.

#2555. Washington Football Heavily Projected to Play in 2026 Sun Bowl

With one game remaining in the regular season, the Washington Huskies are bowl bound, but still unsure of exactly when or where they will play their final game come the postseason.

Based on projections from multiple national media outlets, the Huskies are likely to draw an invite to play in the Sun Bowl against one of three ACC schools: SMU, Pittsburgh or Virginia Tech, when the 2026 rendition of the game kicks off December 31 in El Paso, Texas.

Different from the 2024 game that featured UW and Louisville, a close 35-34 loss for the Huskies, the Sun Bowl is now sponsored by Old El Paso.

In the first Sun Bowl appearance under third-year coach Jedd Fisch, the team nearly completed a 14-point comeback in the fourth quarter, but a failed 2-point conversion in the final seconds that, if completed, would've given UW the victory instead resulted in a 1-point loss to end the 2024 season with a 6-7 record.

If the Huskies are selected to return to El Paso next month it would be their sixth appearance in the Sun Bowl, of which the program has only won once, a 14-7 victory in 1979 over the Texas Longhorns under legendary coach Don James.

Since then UW last lost to 28-6 to Alabama in 1986, 38-18 to Iowa in 1995 and 34-24 to Purdue in 2002 along with the 2024 defeat against Louisville, the longest consecutive streak of losses in a single bowl game in school history narrowly beating out three straight losses in the Holiday Bowl (1996, 99, and 2001) and the Rose Bowl (1926, 1937, and 1944).

Given the Huskies' record in the Lone Star State based bowl game a potential matchup with Pitt, which coincidentally also boasts a 4-1 record all-time against UW, would offer a chance for Fisch to end two losing streaks in one game as the Panthers have come out on top the previous two times they faced each other in 1963 (13-6) and 1979 (26-14).

SMU—which holds the best record of the ACC trio at 7-4—and VT have never faced UW on the football field, posing a pair of unique first-time matchups if either ends up as the Huskies' bowl opponent.

First-year Hokies coach James Franklin did however beat UW twice in his time at Penn State, once against Chris Petersen in the 2017 Fiesta Bowl and most recently against Fisch two years ago in Happy Valley, offering the third-year coach a chance at personal redemption.

Despite the majority of national outlets suggesting UW is bound for El Paso, the team could also draw an invite to the Holiday Bowl in San Diego, which it last made an appearance in 2010 against Nebraska under former coach Steve Sarkisian.

Based on bowl tiers, the Sun Bowl chooses after the Holiday Bowl and before the Poinsettia Bowl, the latter of which UW has never played in, and depending on the outcome of Saturday's regular season finale, could fall to with other games this weekend working against their favor.

#2551. Panthers Injury Report & Transactions Week 12: The Brady Christensen Debacle

The Carolina Panthers front office is busy throughout the season with transactions, roster moves, and injury updates. Here's what's happening at Mint Street this week.

In one of the most baffling decisions in the Dan Morgan general manager era, the Carolina Panthers intentionally placed a reportedly healthy Brady Christensen on the season-ending injured reserve instead of releasing a less experienced, less versatile offensive lineman.

As an armchair GM myself, this highly questionable decision makes zero sense.

Here's what went down before the Panthers front office lost their collective minds.

Brady Christensen was placed on the injured reserve in late August with a hamstring injury. On November 3rd the Panthers opened the 21-day window for Christensen to practice and get back into game action before being reactivated. If a player isn't moved to the active roster at the end of the 21 days, they are required to go on the season-ending IR.

Despite being a healthy, full participant at practice for three straight weeks, the Panthers inexplicably chose not to activate the sixth-year veteran! So, now, one of the most versatile and experienced depth pieces on the Panthers banged-up offensive line can't play this year.

And Brady Christensen is reportedly healthy!

The Panthers have been desperate for quality and depth along an injury prone offensive line all season, and that's exactly what Brady Christensen is: Quality depth! And he can play multiple positions, as well. While he's best at guard, he can slide outside to guard or inside to center when needed. Choosing to put him in mothballs for the rest of the year is perplexing on so many levels.

When explaining why the team chose to end Christensen's season rather than activating him, coach Dave Canales was quoted by the Charlotte Observer as saying, "Brady's ready to go, too. And again, it's just a matter of space on the roster and all those things.

So the 5-5 Carolina Panthers are on track to win the NFC South and make the playoffs and need quality depth across the offensive line, but they shelved Brady Christensen to preserve roster spots for reserve tackle Stone Forsythe? Backup guard Corey Bullock?

Heck, they shut down Brady Christensen to retain No. 5 tight end Felipe Franks instead?

Somebody please make this make sense to me, because right now this looks like the dumbest decision of Dan Morgan's stewardship of the franchise. And if more information comes out later from the Panthers front office detailing Christensen was facing injuries or other circumstances that weren't public, then I'll apologize. But unless this happens, I'm going to hold this over Dan Morgan's head for the rest of the season.

The Panthers injury report looks pretty clean as of Saturday.

The linebacker corps continues to be banged up with Bobby Okereke and Patrick Jones II designated as "out" and reserve Thomas Incoom questionable with a calf injury.

On the offensive side of the ball, running Jonathon Brooks and reserve tight end Felipe Franks are both questionable.

Released DT Cam Horsley from the practice squad

Cam Horsley was signed just over two weeks ago to the practice squad, then released this past week. His NFL resume includes playing in one game for the Tennessee Titans last year, so he'll be looking for his next professional opportunity elsewhere.

Signed and released DT C.J. Ravenell from the practice squad

C.J. Ravenell was signed to the practice squad on Tuesday and released on Wednesday. Man, professional football can be a brutal business.

#2549. Logan Webb landing spots: Five possible destinations for Giants starting pitcher on the trading block

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Coming off a disaster of a season and with a roster badly in need of an overhaul, the Giants make sense as a team to make a trade or two this offseason. Sure enough, they are "listening to trade offers" for All-Star starting pitcher Logan Webb, per The Athletic, but they'd need a "very strong return" in order to deal him.

Webb, 30, has two years and $47 million left on his current deal. He went 8-9 with a 4.31 ERA and 1.3 WAR last season, but it was his worst year in quite a while. He averaged 4.5 WAR per season in the previous four years with a 3.22 ERA and led the National League in innings pitched from 2023 to 2025, racking up three straight top-six Cy Young finishes.

Which teams might make for a good fit for Webb? Many of them. We're talking about a workhorse under team control for two more years. Let's run through five of the best fits while, again, knowing that basically any contender should be interested in at least a conversation with the Giants.

The Cubs need so much pitching this offseason. Their entire rotation heading into the playoffs last season is in free agency. This isn't hyperbole. Matthew Boyd, Shota Imanaga, Kevin Gausman, Clay Holmes and David Peterson are all off the roster. If the Cubs were to try and put together a rotation right now, it would be something like Justin Steele, Edward Cabrera, Javier Assad and several question marks. Ben Brown and Cade Horton will open the season on the injured list.

Do we really need to spell out what a reliable innings eater would mean for this bunch? Webb is an outstanding fit here.

The upstart playoff team last season was a ton of fun, but also was running bullpen games in the ALDS. The White Sox just attached Davis Martin to Luis Castillo in a trade to the Rockies in order to offload Castillo's contract, too, so they're down a starter. The Dustin May signing means they have him along with Sean Burke and converted reliever Grant Taylor. The White Sox would reportedly like to sign another starter in the May ballpark, but what about trading for someone better like Webb?

A top four in the rotation of Webb, Burke, Taylor and May would be exponentially better than what the Sox had last season.

Returns of Spencer Strider and Spencer Schwellenbach at some point will help, but this is still a thin rotation for a team coming off a division title. Chris Sale remains, but he's followed up with Grant Holmes and Bryce Elder before the Spencers return. Youngster Didier Fuentes moving to the rotation is exciting, but there are an awful lot of questions behind Sale, who turns 38 in late March, by the way.

Given that the Padres reside in the NL West with the Giants, there might be a bit of an intradivision tax in terms of the asking price, but Padres boss A.J. Preller is never shy about offloading prospects. There could certainly be a fit. The Padres need rotation help, too, after losing Michael King, Nick Pivetta, Robbie Ray and others to free agency. We know they're in on Tarik Skubal, but that doesn't mean they'll be content with just landing one big fish.

Look at the current Padres rotation. It's basically Joe Musgrove and Randy Vásquez. With three straight playoff berths and zero trips to the World Series, now isn't the time to have Jhony Brito, Ryan Weiss and Ian Koenig make up 60% of the rotation.

Dealing for Webb and signing Skubal would make for a nice offseason for new ownership, no?

One of the most disappointing teams in baseball last season needs to have a prolific offseason. We've heard plenty about the Mets being involved in the Skubal sweepstakes and we've seen them win a monster bidding war before (see: Soto, Juan). Grabbing Webb would make it quite a well-rounded rotation with talented youngsters Nolan McLean, Christian Scott and Zac Thornton.

#2547. Timberwolves, Grizzlies reportedly hope to move to Eastern Conference after expansion; who makes more sense?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA is barreling toward expansion, and the addition of two new teams would have enormous basketball implications for the remaining 30. Perhaps the biggest is geographic. Both Seattle and Las Vegas are located firmly in the western half of the United States. Should those cities eventually be granted teams, they would play in the Western Conference, leaving the league with unbalanced conferences. Therefore, someone in the West would have to move to the East in order to balance the conferences at 16 teams apiece.

Several teams are eager to do so, according to The Athletic. While the New Orleans Pelicans are not out of the running, the likeliest teams to move in realignment, for now, are reportedly the Minnesota Timberwolves and Memphis Grizzlies.

Getting out of the West would be appealing on several levels. Of course, there are obvious basketball reasons for preferring the East. Putting aside the decades of Western Conference superiority that hold little weight in the long run, the two teams best positioned to succeed over the next decade or so are the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder. As the New York Knicks learned last June, the easiest path to a championship is avoiding Victor Wembanyama and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander until they've already spent seven games battling each other.

But this isn't just a basketball conversation. The NBA, like most major American professional sports leagues, tilts east. There are simply more major cities in the Eastern half of the country than the Western half. Of the league's 30 existing teams, 17 play east of the Mississippi River: the 15 already in the Eastern Conference, along with the Timberwolves and Grizzlies.

Travel is simply easier playing in the East. One projection of how many total miles each NBA team will travel this season has only the Miami Heat in the top half of the league, with the other 14 slots belonging to Western Conference teams. That projection has the Heat crossing 24 time zones, while every Western Conference team crosses at least 36.

So Minnesota, Memphis and New Orleans are all incentivized to move, and with the Grizzlies and Timberwolves seemingly favored, let's evaluate the cases for each.

The fundamental case for the Grizzlies is geographic. Memphis is further East than Minneapolis. As The Athletic points out, it is closer to more Eastern Conference teams as well, as it is within 600 miles of five East teams (Charlotte Hornets, Atlanta Hawks, Indiana Pacers, Chicago Bulls and Milwaukee Bucks). This not only makes travel easier for the Grizzlies, but for those teams as well.

While the Timberwolves are considered the better team right now, Memphis is probably the team better positioned to be competitive in the long run. Minnesota's best players -- Anthony Edwards, LaMelo Ball, Jaden McDaniels and Ayo Dosunmu -- are all in their mid-20s earning market-rate salaries, and Rudy Gobert is much older at 34. Plus, the Timberwolves are essentially devoid of first-round draft capital.

The Grizzlies have a significant draft surplus, and their best players -- Cameron Boozer, Cedric Coward and Zach Edey -- are still on their rookie deals. If the idea is balancing the two conferences competitively, even if the Timberwolves have a higher immediate upside, the Grizzlies are probably the team we should expect to contend longer.

And then there's the matter of maintaining established rivalries. While neither the Grizzlies nor the Timberwolves are franchises steeped in historical success, Minnesota's last few years have established the Timberwolves as genuine postseason rivals to several important Western Conference teams. They've faced Nikola Jokiċ and the Denver Nuggets in multiple recent playoff series. They've faced Luka Dončić in multiple recent playoff series, even if they've come against different teams. Their series against the Spurs last spring included a Wembanyama ejection.

The NBA may prefer to maximize the number of games Edwards plays against these high-profile opponents because there are existing narratives surrounding those matchups. In that case, keeping the Timberwolves in the West makes sense while allowing the Grizzlies to shift to the East.

Minnesota's geographic case is a bit more nuanced. While Memphis is closer to more teams, Minnesota is closer to a few geographically convenient ones. If we assume for the moment that the new, 16-team conferences are going to come with four divisions featuring four teams each, Minnesota's proximity to Milwaukee, Chicago and Indiana makes for an easy four-team pod.

The rest of the conference becomes remarkably easy to group from there. We have three more roughly Midwestern teams (Cleveland, Toronto and Detroit), five in the Northeast (New York, Brooklyn, Boston, Philadelphia and Washington) and four in the Southeast (Charlotte, Miami, Orlando and Atlanta). Just move one of those Northeastern teams to the Midwestern group -- presumably Washington, as it doesn't play in the existing Atlantic Division -- and you're set. If the NBA wants to make divisions a more prominent part of scheduling moving forward, Minnesota makes doing so much easier.

There's also the idea of giving Edwards, one of the league's more personable stars, an easier path to the NBA Finals by getting him away from Wembanyama and Gilgeous-Alexander. The NBA is, ultimately, a star business, and if stacking the deck in Edwards' favor helps build him up as one of the faces of the league, there is obvious appeal in doing so.

By all accounts, we are far closer to resolution on a Las Vegas team than to the return of the Sonics in Seattle. Bidding has seemingly been more robust in Las Vegas, and an announcement is expected in the near future. If an announcement on Vegas comes before one in Seattle, there will be a brief period in which the NBA has an odd number of planned franchises.

That does not mean that it will ever actually play a season with only 31 teams. Seattle, as commissioner Adam Silver has described, is much more of a turnkey operation than Las Vegas because of its arena situation and preexisting basketball history. In theory, a Seattle team could be announced much later than a Las Vegas team and still begin play in the same season. For now, the reported target for expansion teams to tip off is the 2028-29 season. However, if Seattle's bidding process takes too long for the two to begin play at the same time, or worse, if no Seattle group manages to put forth an acceptable bid in the near future, the possibility of one or even multiple seasons with 31 teams rather than the expected 32 probably does exist.

The NBA -- and every other major American professional sports league -- has had unbalanced conferences in the past. None do now. It creates scheduling headaches, and it's just blatantly unfair. Forcing some teams to overcome 15 opponents to reach the Finals while others only have to top 14 makes playing in the smaller conference too much of an advantage, and since the conference presently believed to be the superior one (the West) would be getting the Las Vegas team, competitive balance would go from a problem to an outright crisis.

Fans have been calling for the abolition of conferences for decades now. Getting it to actually pass a vote would be harder. Realignment is voted on by the board of governors, so abolishing the conferences theoretically would be as well. Eastern Conference owners love having an easier path to the playoffs and the gate revenue those postseason games generate. This is where the idea of a season or two with just 31 teams in the league carries some appeal. It could give the NBA an opportunity to test the abolition of conferences provisionally with the idea that conferences would return when the league reaches 32 unless a new vote determines otherwise.

The appeal of removing conferences altogether stems from the inherent fairness of a playoff system determined solely by record. There have been concerns about how removing the geographic component of playoff scheduling would affect travel, but there are potential solutions there. Returning to the "2-3-2" home-court format would minimize travel, or higher seeds could be allowed to select opponents in the early rounds to decide for themselves how they'd like to prioritize travel. The odds are obviously against the removal of conferences altogether, but expansion offers a potential opportunity to test it without committing to it long-term, and that's an opportunity the NBA would be foolish not to at least explore.

#2546. MLB rumors: Scott Boras sets Tarik Skubal timeline, plus Tigers signing former Rookie of the Year

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Welcome to Thanksgiving week. Here in Major League Baseball news, that normally means we're bound for a slow week -- save for a few notable exceptions -- but with the CBA expiring on Dec. 1, we might just be in for a free agent frenzy. Let's hope that's the case.

We can start today's set of news and rumors with the biggest free agent out there.

Tarik Skubal is the No. 1 free agent this offseason and the two-time Cy Young winner appears on pace to make a decision before the CBA expires. Skubal's agent, Scott Boras, hit MLB Network Radio on Sunday and said that there's a "strong likelihood" that a decision comes by that Dec. 1 deadline, especially given that Skubal's signing impacts so many other pitchers (Boras mentioned that it impacts "10-15 pitchers").

The 30-year-old lefty was 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA and 186 strikeouts in 158 ⅔ innings last season, as he bounced back after just six weeks from elbow surgery.

The teams most heavily involved in the Skubal rumors to this point have been the Dodgers, Mets, Padres and Blue Jays, all of whom had in-person meetings with him last week.

The Tigers have agreed to a deal with right-hander Luis Gil, per ESPN. It's a one-year, $2.3 million deal.

Gil won the American League Rookie of the Year after a productive 2024 season in which he won 15 games and had a 3.50 ERA, but he spent a good portion of 2026 in the minors and was nontendered by the Yankees on Friday. In his limited MLB time last season, Gil had a 4.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP and 17 strikeouts in 27 ⅓ innings.

The Tigers rotation seems set with Framber Valdez, Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan, so consider Gil a depth option.

The Red Sox also reportedly showed interest.

#2542. Tarik Skubal signing with Mets: Two-time Cy Young winner lands historic nine-year, $450 million contract

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Ace left-hander Tarik Skubal, winner of the last two American League Cy Young awards and far and away the top free agent of the 2026-27 class, has agreed to terms with the New York Mets on a nine-year contract worth $450 million, reports the New York Post. The deal has a $45 million signing bonus with no options or opt-outs, per SNY, as well as a full no-trade clause, so the Mets have locked Skubal up for the full nine years. Further, there are only $30 million in deferrals, according to the New York Post. The deal is pending a physical.

Once finalized, the deal will make Skubal the highest-paid pitcher in Major League Baseball history, in terms of both total contract value and average annual salary.

Skubal, who turned 30 years of age on Nov. 20, is the No. 1 ranked talent on our list of the top 50 free agents for this offseason. Here's part of Mike Axisa's write-up:

"Excluding Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was a special case as a Japanese star with no MLB track record, Skubal is the best starting pitcher to hit free agency since Gerrit Cole in 2019. He showed few long-lasting effects from the NanoScope elbow surgery in May and remains a capital-A Ace with terrific surface stats and under-the-hood performance indicators. Skubal brings four swing-and-miss pitches to the table (four-seamer, changeup, slider, curveball), a near MLB-best ability to limit exit velocity, and elite strike-throwing ability (MLB's third-lowest walk rate since 2023). Build an ace starter in a lab and he would look a lot like Skubal. He'll play the entire 2027 season at age 30, and given the things teams can do with pitchers these days, Skubal figures to remain a frontline starter for most of a long-term contract. He's the only true balance-of-power player available in free agency this offseason. Skubal can swing a division race and a postseason series all by himself."

Over the last three seasons, Skubal has pitched to a 2.42 ERA and an FIP of 2.48 in 546 innings spread over 88 starts. That amounts to a total WAR of 17.7 since the start of the 2024 campaign. Skubal remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and this signing reflects that reality.

Since Skubal was traded to the Los Angeles Dodgers from the Detroit Tigers leading up to the 2026 deadline, he was ineligible to receive the qualifying offer from the Dodgers. As such, the Mets will not be penalized a draft pick for signing Skubal.

The nine years here aren't record-setting, as the longest pitcher contract remains the 12-year deal that Yoshinobu Yamamoto signed with the Dodgers. Yamamoto's $325 million was previously the largest contract for a pitcher -- obviously excepting Shohei Ohtani, as he's a two-way player -- so Skubal's $450 million shatters that record.

Coming off a disappointing 88-loss campaign in 2026, the Mets, big-spending owner Steve Cohen, and lead decision-maker David Stearns needed to make an offseason splash to improve their chances of a 2027 rebound and inspire a perhaps disaffected fan base. Skubal more than qualifies. He'll front a Mets rotation that also includes 25-year-old right-hander Nolan McLean, who himself has frontline long-term potential. In Queens, Skubal joins a roster that also includes the All-Star likes of Juan Soto, Francisco Lindor, and Bo Bichette.

Further, the Mets just locked up young outfielder A.J. Ewing to an eight-year, $95 million extension and we all know plenty about Soto's monster contract. The Mets now have Soto through 2039, Skubal through 2035, Ewing through 2034 and Lindor through 2031.

The rotation for the Mets right now looks something like:

Given the large outlay for Skubal here, the Mets should be all-in on improving the ballclub for the 2027 season, which means we shouldn't expect them to stop with just signing Skubal. That last spot in the rotation, as such, should be ticketed to someone else outside the organization at present, whether a free agent or a trade acquisition.

The landing of the top free agent available no doubt ramps up the pressure on Stearns and the Mets to deliver a playoff berth and a deep October run in 2027, but Skubal's presence also makes it much likely that such a feat comes to pass.

#2539. Falcons release QB Tua Tagovailoa

When the Atlanta Falcons signed Tua Tagovailoa this offseason, he figured to be the starter at the beginning of the season if and when Michael Penix Jr. was not ready to go. Instead, Tua was also hurt when Penix wasn't ready at the beginning of the season and wound up only throwing three passes for the Falcons in 2026, completing two of them for 34 yards and tossing a game-ending interception against the Ravens.

Now, Tua is no longer a Falcon. The Falcons released him Saturday, and will roll forward with Michael Penix Jr., Andy Dalton, and Jack Strand as their three quarterbacks. We'll see how they choose to fill the roster spot.

Tua may have been looking around the league at decimated rosters—the Cardinals are down to their fourth stringer, the Patriots don't have Drake Maye, the Steelers just cut Aaron Rodgers, and so forth—and deciding he wanted a legitimate shot at a starting job somewhere before the season is up. The Falcons, for their part, hadn't gotten much out of Tua and clearly signed Andy Dalton with the thought that he could step into the backup role if they did move on from Tua; after a few weeks with the team, they must feel comfortable with that plan. Strand is a long-term developmental option the team would love to see ascending into the backup role in 2027 or 2028.

The Tua/Falcons marriage made sense at the time of the signing, given that Tua was dirt cheap, has long been an accurate quarterback, and the Falcons needed someone good enough to step in for a while, but not so good that Penix would never have a shot to see the field given the team's investment in him. Unfortunately, Tua never looked more than serviceable during the summer and had ill-timed injuries that kept him from getting on the field; the Baltimore overtime appearance was a maddening microcosm of his career of late with a couple of on=target balls and an inexplicable interception. There are enough quarterback-needy teams out there that a player with Tua's experience and extremely cheap contract might be appealing off of waivers or as a free agent.

For the Falcons, the rest of this season is all about what Penix can or cannot do, and if he's hurt this already struggling team is just going to sink further into the mire regardless of whether Tua is here or not. We'll wish Tua well wherever he lands next, and hope to see Penix catch fire over the final seven weeks.
