Injuries have been one of the defining stories of the young 2026-27 NBA season, and while some teams like the Oklahoma City Thunder are unfortunately months away from relief, others are beginning to see a light at the end of the health tunnel. We're now nearly a month or so out from the early-season wave of losses, and on Friday, ESPN's Shams Charania gave updates on the health of several key absent players. Let's use that as a launching point to check in on a handful of injured stars.

It took Indiana's star point guard a full season to recover from the torn Achilles tendon he suffered in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals, but sadly, his return lasted just four games before he headed back to the sideline. Haliburton was diagnosed with a left hamstring strain in October, and according to ESPN, he will be sidelined for at least the next couple of weeks.

For now, there is no firmer timeline than that, with Pacers coach Rick Carlisle saying in a recent radio interview that he didn't think it was "out of the question" that Haliburton would play in November, but he would not "put a hard date on anything."

Haliburton looked mostly like himself in the four games he played early this season, averaging just under 22 points and 10 assists. The Pacers have fallen to 5-10 and the Eastern Conference's No. 10 seed without him, and they are seemingly aware of the need for reinforcements. The Pacers "clearly are looking at doing something" on the trade market, with an upgrade on the wing viewed as a strong possibility, Jake Fischer said Friday on SiriusXM NBA Radio.

A return to action seems further off for Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards, who had knee surgery in late October. Edwards spoke with reporters Thursday and said he has "no clue" when he'll be able to return to the floor and declined to offer a timetable, per ESPN.

Edwards missed 21 games last year and dealt with a knee issue in the postseason. Despite a hot start, that included a 47-point outburst against the Cavaliers, Edwards continued to experience discomfort in the knee, prompting the team to choose the surgery route rather than have their superstar continue playing through pain.

"It needed to be done in order for me to be able to play without any pain for the next couple years," Edwards said. "But who knows? Maybe in a couple years I might have to get something else. But hopefully not. I think I'll be pretty good."

Led by LaMelo Ball, the Wolves have excelled even in Edwards' absence. At 11-5, Minnesota sits at No. 5 in the Western Conference standings entering their game against the Grizzlies on Saturday.

Leonard has played just twice this season due to knee swelling, but according to Charania, there is optimism that he will return within the next few weeks. Leonard has been dealing with patellar tendinopathy, more commonly known as "jumper's knee," TSN reported on Tuesday. That is the same issue he dealt with throughout his 2019 championship season. SportsNet confirmed that reporting, while noting that swelling is not typically how that injury presents. SportsNet's reporting indicates that the swelling and jumper's knee are separate issues.

The good news on this front is that the reporting to this point indicates that the Raptors do not expect these issues to linger once Leonard returns. Toronto successfully managed Leonard's health through that title season, and is being cautious to start this year as well. However, his absence has certainly been felt as Toronto is in the midst of a six-game losing streak without him.

Meanwhile, the player Leonard was traded for is just about ready to make his Clippers debut. Brandon Ingram is expected to return Monday against the Houston Rockets, according to Charania. Ingram suffered a partially torn Achilles tendon last season, which kept him out of the Clippers' lineup at the start of this year. His absence has been keenly felt in Los Angeles as the Clippers have scuttled to a 4-10 start without him. Los Angeles has both a bottom-eight offense and defense so far this season, so getting Ingram on the court should represent a helpful talent infusion.

San Antonio's second-year star thankfully avoided a major injury when he fell on the court against the Clippers on Thursday. He will, however, miss 1-3 weeks with a left hip rotator strain. Harper was walking without a limp following the injury, per The San Antonio Express-News, a positive sign for his recovery.

The Spurs have the NBA's best record at 13-3, but the story to watch as Harper rests is the performance of former All-Star De'Aaron Fox. Just beginning a four-year max contract, Fox has scored just 23 points in his last three games combined. He's averaging the fewest points and assists of his career since his rookie season. The Spurs had been starting their three high-profile guards -- Fox, Harper and Stephon Castle -- together early in the season. It was working, but with the caveat that that group never played a second without Victor Wembanyama. The Spurs are more than 40 points per 100 possessions better when their MVP candidate is on the floor.

If Fox can't right the ship while Harper is out, that could open the door to San Antonio moving him to the bench upon Harper's return. The Spurs thrived last season with two ball-handlers, two shooters and Wembanyama in their starting lineup. The three guards are working because basically anything works with Wembanyama, but when the competition gets stiffer in the playoffs, it's going to be harder to get away with so little shooting in the starting lineup. That puts the onus on Fox to prove he still belongs in the starting lineup, and bouncing back while Harper is out will be a big part of that.

#2534. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The big prize of this free agent class, ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, has landed with the Mets on a nine-year, $450 million deal.

The knee-jerk reaction to a contract of this size in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the Mets are getting a surefire ace for nearly a decade.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here says this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

Also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a new procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. His nine-year deal means it'll run through his age-38 season.

For those so worried about the long-term finances of the Cohen family, are you sure you're really worried that Skubal won't be productive through five, six or even all nine years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

Justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

David Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

By this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:

Are you sure a 9-year, $450 million deal for this guy is a "risk?"

I think we could argue that it'll be a bargain.

#2533. As James Harden passes Kobe Bryant on NBA's 50-point game list, Donovan Mitchell says he's underappreciated

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

James Harden is in the midst of his worst scoring season since his second year in Oklahoma City 16 years ago, but the 37-year-old turned back the clock some on Friday night with a 51-point performance in a Cavaliers win over the Pacers.

Harden's vintage scoring night saw him go 15-of-26 from the field and 14-of-14 from the free-throw line in typical Harden fashion for the 26th 50-point game of his career. That moves him into third all-time in NBA history for 50-point games, passing Kobe Bryant and sitting just five behind Michael Jordan.

At 37 years old (and 86 days), Harden is the fourth-oldest player to score 50 points in an NBA game, passing LeBron James on that list and trailing only Bryant, Jordan and Jamal Crawford, who scored 50 at 39 years old.

After the game, Cavaliers' coach Kenny Atkinson offered an eyebrow-raising comment calling Harden "top-10 all-time," which drew immediate pushback from NBA fans, but Harden is an unquestioned Hall of Famer and continues to put his name among the all-time greats on NBA scoring lists.

His co-star in Cleveland, Donovan Mitchell, lamented that Harden doesn't get the appreciation he deserves at this stage of his career, and that he expects, much like Russell Westbrook, that it won't happen until he retires.

"He won't until it's over with," Mitchell said. "I hate it, but that's just the world we live in. We won't appreciate greatness. We didn't appreciate Russ in his latter years until now. It's like, 'Oh man, Russ was this and that.' It's like we forgot he averaged 28, 15 and 16 for a month. It's one of those things where we live in such a negative space. I hate it. At the end of the day, he doesn't care. And for me, seeing that, I don't care. It helps, but at the end of the day, that's just what the world is. It sucks that that's that way, but us in this locker room and guys in this league, we know who he is and we know what he's done for the game. That goes for not just him but a lot of people in this league. We don't appreciate what's in front of us on a consistent basis."

Harden has long been a divisive player among NBA fans. Some have appreciated his ruthless efficiency while others have hated the aesthetics of his mastery of the dark arts of drawing fouls. As Mitchell noted, few players have had as much influence over the game in the last decade-plus as Harden. From his massive stepback 3-pointer to his movement on drives to create contact, so much of Harden's game has made its way into the arsenal of most elite guard scorers.

Fans will debate whether that's a good thing, but his influence is undeniable. As Mitchell said, whenever Harden calls it a career, he will get more appreciation, but there will also be heated debates over his place in NBA history as one of the most divisive stars (from a play-style perspective, at least) of his generation.

#2532. All Blacks take revenge on untidy England in Twickenham rain

Tries: Sititi, Roigard Cons: Mo'unga (2) Pens: Mo'unga (4)

New Zealand checked England's resurgence as a smart and disciplined performance in constant rain avenged last weekend's defeat at Allianz Stadium.

After five successive victories and a 37-12 victory over the same opponents seven days ago, England came into the game as rare favourites in a fixture against the All Blacks.

But, with the conditions demanding close-quarters combat and tight discipline to keep the penalty count down, New Zealand adapted far better.

All Blacks number eight Wallace Sititi barged over in the first half, before a clever blind-side snipe by Cam Roigard on the other side of the interval put his side 20-3 to the good.

England's heads never went down. With more than 20 minutes to go, Marcus Smith replaced Fin Smith at fly-half with instructions to chase the game.

However, they seemed caught between attacking via the boot or hand, and made little impression either territorially or on the scoreboard.

Ultimately, New Zealand's carefully built lead, with Richie Mo'unga impeccable off the tee, was sturdy enough to survive easily enough.

Jamie George rumbled over at the back of a late rolling maul for England, but it was too little, too late.

A miserable afternoon for Marcus Smith, whose kicks rarely found his chasers, finished with him slipping as he attempted to convert.

It was a sobering defeat for an England team who have undoubtedly advanced over the autumn, but will start their Six Nations campaign with a trip to Ireland followed by a meeting with defending champions France.

England's indiscipline will feature prominently in head coach Steve Borthwick's review. Alex Coles' 33rd-minute yellow card put them under pressure either side of the break. Henry Pollock's sin-binning for offside on 65 minutes wrote off whatever faint hopes there were of a comeback. Twelve penalties, although fewer than the 14 conceded by their opponents, also undercut their efforts.

After defeat by Wales a fortnight ago, New Zealand vented their frustration in victory with prop Ethan de Groot replicating Seb Atkinson's 'cut-throat' celebration at the end of one defensive set and Rieko Ioane barking in Jack van Poortvliet's face.

Their victory, watched by 60,040 people, is the first by a southern hemisphere side in the Nations Championship finals weekend.

The title will be contested by France and South Africa on Sunday evening.

Marcus Smith was introduced to try and haul the game back England's way but could not spark his side into life [Getty Images]

After former captain Lewis Moody had been at the centre of the haka response before last weekend's victory, England replied to Ioane and his team-mates' challenge by marching up to halfway as one.

It was clear that their tactics would have to be different in the game as well.

With the rain teeming down, ambitions were reined in and shots at goal taken.

The game was only a couple of minutes old when Henry Slade called for the tee and landed a long-range penalty from halfway to put the hosts on the board.

That turned out to be England's only entry on the scoreboard for more than 70 minutes.

The premium on points was high, with the ball soapy and phases difficult to build. Physicality was also to the fore.

Ellis Genge went nose to nose with De Groot in the aftermath of an early penalty call against England and, shortly after, continued the conversation with a massive hit that flattened his fellow loosehead.

New Zealand though, uncharacteristically listless in defeat last week, brought more intent and venom to the gainline.

England's kick-chase, a tactic that was key to a winning run through 2025 and well suited to the wet conditions, was dusted off. However, in the tight early exchanges, it also risked a rare bit of broken field for either side.

When Van Pootvliet's 16th-minute box-kick bobbled out of the aerial contest, Ioane pounced on the loose ball and made a half-break that put England back on their heels.

New Zealand maintained their momentum and their attack ended with Sititi, with Jordie Barrett providing a boost from behind, shunting over from close range.

Jordie Barrett, the one All Black who showed up well last weekend, led from the front again, putting in one huge hit to stop Ben Earl, England's chief ball carrier, in his tracks.

With the visitors applying pressure in the scrum, England found themselves forced further and further back. Their defence was courageous. A combination of Joe Heyes and Luke Cowan-Dickie prised themselves under Anton Segner to hold the flanker up over the tryline.

However, England's discipline, much improved this autumn, frayed under the pressure.

Second row Coles was sin-binned after failing to dip and catching Fabian Holland high in the tackle.

When Tommy Freeman threw the ball away, preventing Josh Moorby taking a quick line-out after Roigard's excellent 50:22, there was a danger of heads and games being lost simultaneously.

Mo'unga slotted the subsequent penalty to send his team down the tunnel 10-3 to the good.

Roigard's blind-side snipe, brushing aside opposite number Van Pootvliet and diving in, had England on the ropes shortly after.

Borthwick pulled the pin on his power-loaded bench, with George Martin introduced among four replacements in the immediate aftermath of Roigard's score.

The hosts had opportunties which could have been the launchpad for a comeback.

Most notably, Freeman and Will Joseph were left waiting for a pass that never came when Freddie Steward went through.

But New Zealand remained out of reach as England's kicking game was too often and too long, gifting possession away and eating up the clock.

Grumbles swirled around the stadium stands as Marcus Smith played a game that seemed counter to his natural ball-in-hand instincts.

England's ability to think on the fly and find a way into the game went astray when, for the first time this autumn, they came under scoreboard pressure.

After three wins, this result will be the one which provides the most lessons from November.

#2530. Hope is now gone for Cowboys' season after historic Thanksgiving collapse vs. Eagles

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ARLINGTON, Texas -- AT&T Stadium went from a full-throated roar to so deathly quiet that one could hear a scoop of cranberry sauce drop with two seconds remaining on the clock on Thanksgiving Day.

When Philadelphia Eagles kicker Jake Elliott's 59-yard field goal sailed through the uprights to complete a 21-point comeback, the largest Thanksgiving comeback in NFL history, the sensation Dallas Cowboys owner/general manager Jerry Jones felt when the stadium scoreboard read "Eagles 39, Cowboys 38" was numb. Nothingness. Emptiness. "Numbing" was the feeling Jones kept going back to outside the locker room postgame.

"The word is numbing. Numbing at the end," Jones said postgame. "I didn't expect to be having this kind of conversation with you guys about 10 minutes left in that game."

The Cowboys (5-7) desperately needed a win on Thanksgiving to get back to .500 and maintain a spot nipping at the heels of the NFC East-leading New York Giants (6-3-1). They were well on their way to doing so after quarterback Dak Prescott's 12-yard scoring strike out to running back Javonte Williams put Dallas on top 28-10 at halftime. Following kicker Brandon Aubrey draining a 59-yard field goal with 3:35 left in the third quarter, the Cowboys' lead ballooned to 21.

Then, everything came crashing down. Eagles fill-in quarterback Joe Milton, one of Dallas' backup quarterbacks up until October when the Eagles signed him off of the Dallas practice squad, carved the Cowboys up like Thanksgiving turkey, throwing for 331 yards and an interception on 21-of-31 passing with a 15-yard rushing touchdown. He hit on touchdown passes of 50 yards and 45 yards to wide receiver DeVonta Smith (200 yards receiving and two touchdowns on 11 catches) as well as on a 24-yarder to rookie first-round pick wide receiver Makai Lemon. No defense could have possessed a greater understanding of an opposing quarterback's tendencies than Milton, someone they worked against every day in practice as their scout team quarterback up until just over a month ago.

Oh, and this happened against an Eagles team (4-7) that is a husk of the squad that steamrolled the entire league en route to a Super Bowl title at the end of the 2024 season. They entered Thanksgiving Thursday without Super Bowl MVP quarterback Jalen Hurts (blood clots) and All-Pro linebacker Zack Baun (back). They also lost running back Saquon Barkley (stinger), cornerback Cooper DeJean (concussion) and tight end Dallas Goedert (shoulder) during the game. Six-time Pro Bowl right tackle Lane Johnson retired in-season a number of weeks ago. It didn't matter.

Aubrey, who signed a four-year, $28 million extension with $20 million guaranteed that made him the NFL's highest-paid kicker this past offseason, missed a 40-yard field goal that would have put the Cowboys up 11 with 3:42 left to play. A blocked punt returned for a touchdown made the Eagles believe they could come back with the margin trimmed down to seven, with 13:46 left to play.

After the special teams' shakiness, coach Brian Schottenheimer decided to put the football in Prescott's hands on a game-clinching fourth-and-1 at the Eagles' 39 with 55 seconds remaining. However, Prescott got sacked for a nine-yard loss, and the Eagles' next drive ended with Elliott's game-winner with two seconds left on the clock.

Prescott was left stunned and agreed with Jones that numb was an appropriate way to describe his postgame emotions. The light was clearly gone from the ever-resilient and optimistic quarterback's eyes at his postgame press conference. After all, his 2026 Cowboys are the only team in NFL history to average over 30 points per game (31.3 points per game, the second most in the NFL this season) and have a losing record through 12 games, according to CBS Sports Research.

"Pretty stunning," Prescott said. "[Numb is] a good description for how I'm feeling right now. Yeah, especially this soon after the game, understanding the plays left out there, the plays we could have made, should have made and the mistakes we had."

Perhaps the most deflating part of Dallas blowing a 14-plus-point lead at home against a team with a losing record is that this wasn't the Cowboys' first time doing so. Prior to November, Dallas was 202-0-1 when leading by that much in the fourth quarter at home in the 67-season existence of Cowboys football. Fast forward to Thanksgiving, and the Cowboys have lost twice this month in that situation against rebuilding teams with backup quarterbacks.

Dallas allowed Gardner Minshew and the NFC West bottom-feeding Arizona Cardinals (3-8) to dig out of a 24-10 hole and win 33-30 in overtime. That was the worst loss of the 2026 season until Thursday. The Cowboys don't play again for 11 more days when they suit up again in Seattle against the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks (6-4) on "Monday Night Football." This is one of the rare cases where having more time to process the grief from a letdown loss might be a bad thing.

"Hopefully it helps, but it's definitely going to sting during it and particularly these next couple of days," Prescott said of the 11-day layoff. "But as we get back into the building, we can't allow this to hold us back."

The problem for Dallas is that the Cardinals and Eagles home losses are hardly the only soul-crushing defeats of the year. Here's a quick rundown if you've lost count.

Days after the 49ers loss, Schottenheimer stripped first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker of defensive play-calling duties while still keeping him on the coaching staff. He gave defensive play-calling to Parker's mentor Mike Pettine, who was recently hired on staff out of retirement as a senior defensive assistant.

The hits just keep on coming, and this latest one prevented Dallas from getting back to .500 at 6-6 ahead of playing the NFL's second-toughest remaining strength of schedule. Their final five opponents have a combined winning percentage of .608, so this loss essentially erased all hope for an NFC East division title run.

"The message shouldn't have to motivate you, shouldn't have to inspire," Prescott said about how to keep the team together. "It shouldn't be the reason that you go win, or the message wasn't good enough, and it's the reason that we lost. So there's got to be a sense of accountability that doesn't fall on the messenger."

* First team ever with two home losses in a season up 14-plus points in the fourth quarter, per CBS Sports Research

Dallas surrendered 22 fourth-quarter points on defense to an Eagles team that hadn't scored more than that amount in an entire game since Week 2, Philadelphia's last game before their seven-game losing streak ended in Week 11 against the Pittsburgh Steelers, which ended up imploding that franchise.

The Cowboys' 2026 season isn't officially over, but it might as well be. Games at the 2025 NFC finalists — the Seahawks (6-4) and Los Angeles Rams (7-4) — loom, as do matchups with the AFC South-leading Jacksonville Jaguars (7-3), the Giants (6-3-1) and the surging Washington Commanders (4-5-1). Dallas has too much scar tissue, both mentally and physically, to realistically get back into the NFC East race.

"I mean, it's a gut check for sure. Told the guys that," Schottenheimer said postgame. "Division football. That's what we talked about in the locker room."

Prescott said everyone from the top down in the Cowboys franchise needs to take some time off this weekend before hitting the ground running.

"And [we have to] get back to it with more urgency and better than ever individually and collectively to give it our best chance," Prescott said.

But are these battered and scarred Cowboys able to successfully respond and bounce back from yet another gut-wrenching loss? The face of the franchise quarterback who is tasked with being Mr. Perfect on and off the field in Dallas couldn't answer that question definitively.

Prescott likely couldn't do so because, deep down, he already knows: The 2026 season will go down as another year of his prime wasted in another lost Cowboys campaign. That's why that numbing feeling is setting in for Jones and his Cowboys once again.

#2529. Winners and losers of the Tarik Skubal signing: Blue Jays, Dodgers strike out; David Stearns looks nervous

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The best player in a thin free agent class came off the board Sunday evening. Two-time Cy Young winning left-hander Tarik Skubal has agreed to a record nine-year, $450 million contract with the New York Mets. There's a $45 million signing bonus and $30 million in deferred payments. The team has not yet announced the signing but that should happen soon.

The $450 million contract shatters the previous record for a pitcher, which is Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million contract with the Dodgers, Skubal's most recent team. The $50 million average annual salary also shatters the previous record for a pitcher. That was $43.3 million for Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander during their time with the Mets.

Here now are our winners and losers from Skubal's monster contract with the Mets.

Let's start with the obvious: Skubal's a winner because he signed a massive, record-shattering contract. Sign a record deal and you're always a winner in my book. The Mets are a winner because they landed not just the best free agent on the market, but one of the game's best pitchers. Skubal is a power player who can swing a postseason race or a postseason series all by himself. There are very few players like that in the game and now the Mets have one to lead their rotation.

Boras, Skubal's agent, tends to shatter records, not beat them by just a little bit. Alex Rodriguez's contract with the Rangers is his Mona Lisa: A-Rod's $252 million contract was exactly double the largest contract in the four major North American sports leagues at the time (Kevin Garnett's $126 million deal with the Minnesota Timberwolves). Boras did it again with Skubal. He obliterated Yamamoto's total guarantee record, Scherzer's and Verlander's shared average annual value record, and also Max Fried's record deal for a lefty ($218 million). Once again, Boras won big.

We can add the Padres here too since they were one of the four teams to meet with Skubal in person this past week, though it was always hard to see San Diego beating out the Blue Jays, Dodgers, and Mets. The Dodgers reportedly held the line at a short-term, high-dollar contract similar to Kyle Tucker's deal, which put them at a disadvantage. Still, they no longer have Skubal in their rotation, and he's irreplaceable. The Blue Jays have been trying to sign top free agents for years (Tucker, Shohei Ohtani, Juan Soto, etc.) and have yet to land the plane. Point is, these teams met and pursued Skubal, then he signed elsewhere. Ergo, losers.

With Skubal off the board, the market for second- and third-tier free agent starters should quickly pick up. That group includes Michael King, Freddy Peralta, and Trevor Rogers. Skubal signing this early is a big win for everyone, really, and especially the other free agent starters. They have more than a week to negotiate and sign before the owners are expected to lock out the players after the current CBA expires at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1. Pitchers are coming off the board fast and furious right now. Expect that to continue for another week or so.

To be sure, the Mets' president of baseball operations is a winner because his team now employs Skubal. This is 100% a Steve Cohen contract, though. Stearns has been against long-term contracts for pitchers throughout his career as an executive, even if he said during the GM Meetings that he works on a "case-by-case basis," and it's hard to believe he'd give a pitcher with three elbow surgeries on his resume this contract. It seems likely Cohen was the one pushing this deal across the finish line, and hey, he's the owner; he can do whatever he wants. Stearns is very much against long-term deals for pitchers, though. I imagine he feels at least a wee bit nervous. Plus, he really can't afford another disaster season like 2026.

Once again, the top free agent went with a big market team. The Mets are signing Skubal this offseason. The Dodgers signed Tucker last offseason. The Mets signed Soto the offseason before that. The Dodgers signed Ohtani the offseason before that. The folks who insist baseball needs a salary cap, both the owners themselves and the fans who lean that way, now have more ammunition for their fight. Settle in. It is very, very likely we're in for months of salary cap debate during an extended lockout. That was true even before Skubal signed.

Among sports fans, Carmelo Anthony is perhaps most synonymous with New York -- both upstate from his incredible year at Syracuse and in New York City, where he starred for the Knicks. But Anthony was raised in Baltimore and is extremely proud of his roots.

So when Baltimore Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey made headlines this week when he said that the thing the city of Baltimore was best at creating was "criminals," Anthony felt compelled to respond. Humphrey was admonished by the Ravens, which sent him home for the week and will hold him out on Sunday against the Carolina Panthers. He also received scathing responses from Baltimore Mayor Brandon Scott and many other prominent Baltimore figures.

Anthony joined that group on Friday with an Instagram post that called on Humphrey to go beyond the apology he issued earlier in the week. Anthony wants Humphrey to join him, Scott, and others in the community to find ways to lead by example.

I've been sitting with this one for a couple of days, because Baltimore isn't a talking point to me. It's in my blood. I came up on Myrtle Avenue in West Baltimore. I saw what this city can take fro you. I lost friends to the streets, and I watched people I loved get swallowed by a system that was built to swallow them. I know the reputation. I've heard every joke and every headline my whole life.

So when one of our own stands on our name and says the best thing Baltimore makes is criminals, and then laughs that it'll get cut out, that doesn't get cut out for me. It doesn't get cut out for the kid in Baltimore who heard it. It doesn't get cut out for the mother working two jobs to keep her son off the corner. And it doesn't get cut out for the man who did his time, came home, and is fighting every day to be seen as more than his worst moment.

Marlon, I see the apology. I'll take it, man to man. But Baltimore has been apologized to its whole life. Apologies don't build anything. Presence does. I put my time, energy and resources in Baltimore because I want kids to have somebody who believe in them. That's the job when you wear this city on your chest. You don't get to rep Baltimore on Sundays and talk about it like an outsider on Wednesday.

So let me tell you what Baltimore makes. We make fighters. We make builders. We make people who were counted out from the day they were born and showed up anyway. We make teachers who buy supplies out of their own pockets, coaches who become fathers, artists the whole world copies, and returning citizens who turn their pain into purpose. We make Olympians, Hall of Famers, legends. We make ME. We make Tank Davis.

The Mayor opened a door. Walk through it. And when you do, call me. I'll meet you there. Let's sit with these young boys together and let them hear from two men who wear this city that they are not what anybody says they are.

Baltimore doesn't make criminals. Baltimore makes the ones who make it out. And the ones who come back. #B-MORE.

The overwhelming response to Humphrey's comments in Baltimore has been to highlight the incredible work being done by leaders to improve conditions, decrease violence, and provide mentorship and guidance to young people in the city.

Anthony echoed the mayor's invitation to join in that work in the community and offered to be there right alongside him.

#2526. Tom Brady torches Aaron Rodgers for 'private things becoming public' after Steelers' release

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

From one future Pro Football Hall of Famer to another, Tom Brady was disappointed by Aaron Rodgers' comments this week leading to his release from the Pittsburgh Steelers. After the team announced it was benching Rodgers for Mason Rudolph on Tuesday night ahead of Friday's game against the Denver Broncos, Rodgers publicly lashed out at coach Mike McCarthy, embarrassing him on a national stage.

Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep during team meetings, not being on task on the job and failing to connect with players. Brady said "nobody wins when the family feuds" and disagreed with how Rodgers handled the situation.

"In response to that, the sanctity of an NFL locker room is a very sacred place, and we should never lose track of that as players," Brady said during the second half of Thursday's Eagles-Cowboys game. "It's a privilege to be in that locker room. You're fighting with your teammates. You're fighting coaches. You're always acting as a team together. It shouldn't always be the place for private things to become public; that's what I'll say."

Brady, who went 3–2 in his career against the former longtime Green Bay Packers quarterback, including a 31–26 victory in the 2021 NFC Championship Game, said Rodgers' admissions were selfish given his role on the team.

"Certainly a Hall of Fame career, and he's a tremendous player, and it has nothing to do with his play style," Brady said. "I was fortunate to be around a lot of great teammates over the years, and what made a great teammate to me was, you cared about your teammates and your coaches and you cared about what the team was trying to accomplish.

"And that supersedes any individual aspect of your game that you want to promote. I was in a great locker room. I played for my teammates, I played for my coaches."

McCarthy took the high road hours after Rodgers' remarks this week.

"He has a lot of opinions, and there's things we've always talked about. I considered those private conversations," McCarthy said before Friday's game with the Broncos. "There's a long history there. Clearly [a] difference of opinion."

McCarthy and Rodgers were part of a braintrust in Green Bay that lasted 13 seasons, including a Super Bowl XLV victory in 2011. McCarthy said his only focus this week was beating the Broncos and said this team had the "opportunity to grow today because of the things that were said" from Rodgers.

"And all those teammates have to — they're going to go and regroup, and that's going to hopefully galvanize them toward, you know, you feel like you're in the foxhole together," Brady said.

Former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin called the dispute between Rodgers and McCarthy a "dumpster fire" and expressed "general sadness" that the relationship between professionals would end this way.

"Sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career in the quarterback Aaron Rodgers, and just at the macro level whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum," Tomlin said Wednesday on The Pat McAfee Show. "Those are things that kind of run counterculture to professional football."

#2525. So you missed out on Tarik Skubal: The best starting pitchers still available through free agency, trade

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Mets' splash record signing of ace lefty Tarik Skubal, who was far and away the top free agent available, has of course reset the market in a major way. Those who missed out on Skubal and those aspiring contenders who otherwise have rotation needs may be left wondering: What's next?

Clubs like the Chicago Cubs, Atlanta Braves, San Diego Padres, Los Angeles Dodgers, Chicago White Sox, Tampa Bay Rays, among others, still have options, even if none of them rise to the skyscraping level of Mr. Skubal. Let's explore some possibilities for you, and let's also move beyond just the current class of free agents and name-check some potential trade targets who could buttress a rotation for next season and beyond. Let's jump in.

Yes, Morejon is a reliever at this writing, but his deep repertoire, excellent velocity and stuff make him a compelling transition candidate for next season, even with recent reporting that he wants to stay in the bullpen. Morejon, who sits triple digits, can give some velocity back while working longer outings and still have plenty in the tank to miss bats in the strike zone. And if starting doesn't work, he can go right back to dominating as a reliever. He doesn't turn 28 until February.

While his ERA ballooned last season thanks to some early season struggles, Rogers' underlying performance indicators are still quite strong, specifically his ability to get chase out of the zone and duck quality contact with four pitches (four-seamer, sinker, changeup, sweeper) that light up analytical models. Rogers also has a fifth-pitch cutter and has shown the ability to hammer the strike zone the last two years. He's not a name that leaps readily to mind, but Rogers has a high ceiling and bargain potential.

Peralta, coming off three straight seasons for the Milwaukee Brewers in which he topped 30 starts and 200 strikeouts, wasn't himself with the New York Mets for the first half-plus of 2027. However, after a deadline trade to the Rays, he made some adjustments and re-established himself as a highly useful starter, all the way to ALCS MVP. The market's going to reflect his rediscovered form. The 2027 season will be his age-31 campaign.

He has a full, five-pitch repertoire with elite spin and movement on almost all of those five offerings and boasts an ERA+ of 129 for his career. King turns 32 in May, and he's experienced a gradual decline at the command-and-control level over the past few seasons. As well, his fastball's not beating hitters in the zone like it used to. That's to say, there's risk here, but even if he's beginning his decline phase, King will be a rotation asset for the near- to mid-term.

The 32-year-old righty was reborn last season after a deadline trade to the Braves. Atlanta ramped up his splitter usage and adjusted his slider shape, and in perhaps related matters, Mahle was much more successful at staying away from the heart of the zone. In 54 ⅓ innings after the trade, Mahle ran a sub-2.00 ERA and struck out 48 batters against nine walks. No, he's not going to put up those numbers over the long haul, but his revival makes him an intriguing option.

The big pre-Skubal hot stove news was the San Francisco Giants' reported willingness to listen to offers on ace Logan Webb. Webb, who just recently turned 30, endured a bit of a down 2026 on the run-prevention front, but the overall body of work remains very strong. For his career, the three-time All-Star has a career ERA+ of 115 with three top 10 finishes in the American League Cy Young vote. In three of the past four seasons, he's topped 200 innings. Webb is under contract through 2028.

Will the Rays part with him even though they're the defending American League champs? They're famously comfortable with churning core contributors, and McClanahan is going into his walk year in 2027. McClanahan's long and labored comeback from Tommy John surgery was finally realized this past season, and he turned in a strong age-29 campaign for the Rays. He was pretty much an ace from 2021-23 before the elbow problems took hold.

Teams will pay a lot for a young and controllable starting pitcher with frontline upside, and all of that describes the 27-year-old lefty Detmers. Not eligible for free agency until after the 2028 season, Detmers topped 4.0 WAR this past season and struck out 211 batters in 185 innings. For the Halos, trading him might be an example of selling high, but the pending change in ownership clouds any reading of those particular tea leaves.

Greene has one of the biggest fastballs in the game and a top 10 finish in the NL Cy Young balloting in his recent past. However, he's struggled to stay healthy and realize his potential on a sustained basis – the potential that made him the No. 2 overall draft pick in 2017. He's signed through 2028 with a club option for 2029, and it may be time for a change of scenery. He's been the subject of trade speculation before, and this winter figures to be no exception.

Yes, deGrom is 38, but going into the final guaranteed year of his contract, he remains capable of being a solid rotation presence for a contender. deGrom reportedly used his full no-trade clause to block a swap to the Braves at the deadline, so it's far from certain whether he'd be willing to approve a deal out of Arlington. That said, such things are always negotiations, and a late-career run at the playoffs might prove tempting for him.

#2524. Is Stephen Curry the real NBA MVP? It's hard not to think so when you watch the Warriors without him

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

It's easy to forget because of what Stephen Curry has turned the Golden State Warriors into over the last decade and change, but this is an organization with some pathetic history in its books. So it's really saying something to start registering all-time marks of franchise ineptitude, which is precisely what the Warriors have done over the last week.

After battling admirably in a respectable loss to the Houston Rockets on the night Curry went down with an oblique injury in the first quarter, the Warriors have lost their last four games by 20-plus points for just the second time in franchise history. The only other time this has happened to a Warriors team was in February of 1998, a few months after Latrell Sprewell choked P.J. Carlesimo. The total margin of that four-game losing streak was 104 points.

This current one is even worse. These Warriors have lost their last four by 109 points, and what makes it even more jarring is comparing them to the team that had won eight straight prior to Curry's injury. That 1997-98 team was trash all year, starting 1-14 and finishing with just 19 wins without ever winning more than three straight games.

These Warriors, on the other hand, were starting to look like a legitimate playoff-caliber team. A cynic would say that run of victories came against a softer schedule than what they have faced of late, but that qualification doesn't hold much, if any, water. That eight-game run included wins over the Denver Nuggets, Minnesota Timberwolves, Los Angeles Lakers, Miami Heat and an Orlando Magic team that has immediately gone on to win five of its last six.

Perhaps the Warriors would have lost to the 13-3 San Antonio Spurs even with Curry. Hell, maybe they would've lost to the New Orleans Pelicans, Dallas Mavericks and Memphis Grizzlies, too. That feels unlikely, but who knows? Even with Curry, the Warriors aren't good enough to start checking off scheduled wins. But that's not the point.

The point is how utterly incapable they have looked in losing these games. Not only have they lost each of these last four by at least 20 points, but they've also been held under 100 points in all of them. That's a combination of incompetence that stretches beyond a franchise mark. That hasn't happened to a single other team this century.

Before we try to answer that, let's just agree upfront that Curry has little to no chance of actually winning what would be his third MVP. The Warriors almost certainly won't have a good enough record to put him in real contention. His across-the-board counting stats, even if he were to maintain his torrid early pace, are not going to match those of Luka Dončić or Victor Wembanyama.

The only real chance would be if both of those guys, and likely a bunch of others, failed to meet the 65-game threshold, but the chances of Curry, who has already missed six games and isn't expected to be re-evaluated until around Thanksgiving, making it to 65 games himself already feel next to impossible. He may be past the maximum 17 games-missed mark before he even returns from this injury.

Which is to say, what we're asking here is whether Curry, at 38 years old and in his 18th season, is still the most valuable player in the league (has he always been?), not whether he'll actually win the award, and the answer to that question, at least in its simplest form, could very well lie in his absence. Just look at this team without him.

Admittedly, there's some cherry-picking in those numbers. Curry actually didn't play in one of the wins during that eight-game streak, and the Warriors still beat the Los Angeles Clippers 124-112 with a 122.8 offensive rating behind 37 points from rookie Yaxel Lendeborg.

We're also leaving out the aforementioned game against the Rockets on Nov. 11 in which Curry only played six minutes and the Warriors looked fine, or even good, in testing one of the best teams in the league to its limit. It also must be noted that Golden State lost its first three games of the season and looked every bit like the team many of us predicted would stink, all of which Curry played in.

Still, the general rule applies. The Warriors go as Curry goes. That was true even in the golden years when the on/off splits, even with the likes of Kevin Durant and Klay Thompson still out there, always pointed to Curry as the clear MVP.

"If I didn't have Steph, I would've been like every other NBA coach and lasted a few years [with the Warriors] and then gone and coached somewhere else," Steve Kerr has said, openly admitting that Curry, and Curry alone, has been the difference between a journeyman coaching career and a Hall-of-Fame one.

He's not lying. Have a look at the numbers.

Even if you want to remove the 2019-20 season from the equation, when Durant had defected, Thompson missed the whole year and Curry only played in five games, Kerr is still a below-.500 coach at 74-96 without Curry in the lineup. This is a coach who has had all kinds of great players at his disposal over the years, and still it was always Curry in control of his and the organization's ultimate fate.

This is still the case for the Warriors, who continue to fall off a cliff without Curry. When he's been on the floor this year, they have registered a 59.6 eFG%, which would rank first in the league. When he's off, they fall to 49.1%, which would rank last.

Even the defensive decline we see in Curry's on/off splits can largely be tied back to his offense. Without him, the Warriors are unable to create the same shots and, when their new brand of shots miss far more often, they end up defending in transition on almost 3% more possessions. That's a big deal. It's meant almost five more points per game surrendered to fast breaks over this stretch.

The Warriors have produced an average offensive rating of 103.8 in games Curry hasn't played this year, which would rank as the second-worst mark in the league. All told, they are 26.3 points per 100 possessions better in Curry's minutes this season, per Cleaning The Glass. By comparison, the Lakers drop by 25.5 points per 100 when Dončić sits. Wembanyama is in his own galaxy with this stat, representing a 37.8-point decline in San Antonio when he's off the floor.

It's fair to say Wembanyama means as much to San Antonio's defense, where most of that decline happens, as Curry does to Golden State's offense, and certainly the Lakers falling off by as much as they do offensively, even with Austin Reaves as a legit secondary star, tells you everything you need to know about his impact. All of these guys are MVP players.

But only one, by subjective definition, can be the most valuable, and the simple truth is the Lakers and Spurs are outfitted with far more functional rosters independent of their respective superstars. In Golden State, there is just nowhere else to turn. Nobody to generate any kind of consistent offensive leverage. No gravity. No shot creation.

After the Warriors took that 38-point beating against the Spurs without Curry, the rookie Lendeborg, who had, in total unfairness, been saddled with filling Curry's go-to-scorer shoes, said "it felt helpless out there," and that is exactly what it has looked like since the Curry variable was removed from Golden State's equation.

To be fair, the absence of a player is an imperfect lens through which to view value for a bunch of contextual reasons, not the least of which is how a team like Golden State is designed to play -- a specific, Curry-centric ecosystem not particularly amenable to abrupt adjustments. These players are not as bad as they have looked without Curry over these last four games.

But by the same token, they aren't close to as good as they looked with Curry, either. I always laugh when my dad calls me saying things like, "This Pat Spencer guy can play!" Everyone looks like they can play next to Curry. And then he goes away and suddenly you're wondering how the hell this guy made the Washington Generals look like one of the best teams in the league. Is he some kind of miracle worker?

In a basketball sense, that's not far off. Curry's individual production is already virtually unmatched, but it's his exponential powers, his ability to compound the returns of those around him, that set him apart. It's early, yes. Perhaps the Warriors will figure things out the longer Curry is away. Probably not. But maybe they at least can return to competitive functionality. Until then, however, it's pretty hard to not think Curry is the most valuable player in the league when you watch the Warriors play without him.

On Tuesday, Aaron Rodgers was benched. On Wednesday, he was released after going on national television and claiming his head coach was a narcoleptic, unhealthy, lazy man who still thinks he coaches the Green Bay Packers. On Friday, the Pittsburgh Steelers have to play the Denver Broncos.

This is a moment where the locker room rallies together and puts out the fire that Rodgers set inside their building, or they completely fall apart, and Mike McCarthy is a one-and-done. Which side are you taking? The Steelers have won and covered in six straight home games. Friday seems like an appropriate time for that streak to end.

The Broncos are coming off one of their best games of the season, as they scored a season-high 38 points while handing the Las Vegas Raiders a 14-point defeat. Rookie running back Jonah Coleman rushed for 111 yards and three touchdowns in that matchup. Give me the Broncos in a gross game.

The pick: Broncos -4.5Projected score: Broncos 20-13

I'm not going to change my tune on the Minnesota Vikings after they were dominated by the San Francisco 49ers in Mexico City. Maybe I will if they mess up this get-right opportunity against an Atlanta Falcons team that has lost three straight. Remember, this is a revenge game for Kirk Cousins. He signed a four-year, $180 million deal with Atlanta in 2024, and the Falcons turned right around and drafted Michael Penix Jr. at No. 8 overall that year. Cousins went 7-7 in 2024, then reentered the lineup in 2025 and helped the Falcons finish the year on a 5-2 run.

Seven points is a large number when you consider that the Under seemingly always hits in these Vikings games. The Under has cashed in nine straight games and in 17 of Minnesota's last 19. Still, I think the Vikings get back on track at home in this spot.

How about those Washington Commanders? That 22-20 comeback win against the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday night was impressive. A win on Sunday will get Washington to .500 for the first time this season, and it's important because the Commanders aren't out of the NFC East race just yet.

Despite the 4-5-1 record, I think Jayden Daniels is playing some pretty great football. He has the second-most 20-yard completions (18) in the NFL since Week 8 and is generating an explosive play on 11.8% of dropbacks since that mark. It's the fifth-best rate in the NFL in that timeframe. Washington isn't exactly loaded with weapons, but the rookie Antonio Williams is really coming on. He caught nine of 11 targets for 122 yards last week vs. Cincy and set up the game-winning field goal.

As for the Arizona Cardinals, it looks like Josh Johnson will be starting again with Carson Beck still out with a back injury. The Cardinals have lost their last three games by at least 14 points and their last two by at least 27 points.

The pick: Commanders -6.5Projected score: Commanders 26-17

I imagine Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold will return this week after missing the last two games with a quad injury. Drew Lock has created a bit of a quarterback controversy since he's won all four of the games he's played the majority of, while Darnold is 2-4 if we throw out that season opener where he left early. Darnold has accounted for 10 touchdowns compared to nine interceptions.

The 49ers are coming off a trip to Mexico City where they dominated the Vikings by 25(!) points. I had the 49ers as a best bet last week, but I didn't expect that. Brock Purdy did suffer an ankle injury that held him out of practice on Wednesday and Thursday, but I'm banking on him playing. (Plus, Mac Jones is the best backup QB in the NFL).

You should know that the 49ers are 0-9 against the spread in their last nine home divisional games. However, they've only played one divisional game at Levi's Stadium this year, and that came in Week 3 against the Cardinals. The 49ers won by six points, failing to cover the 8.5-point spread. But with this number at a field goal, I think the 49ers have a good chance to end that streak this week.

#2520. What's next for the Mets after record-breaking deal with Tarik Skubal? Biggest needs for 2027

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The New York Mets landed the offseason's best free agent and one of the game's top pitchers Sunday evening. The Mets and two-time Cy Young-winning lefty Tarik Skubal have agreed to a record-shattering nine-year contract worth $450 million. The contract obliterates the previous pitcher records for total guarantee (Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million) and average annual value (Max Scherzer's and Justin Verlander's $43.3 million). A 1-of-1 contract for a 1-of-1 pitcher.

New York's offseason work is not complete, however. It's not close to complete, really. The Mets went 74-88 and disappointed every which way this past season. There are still roster needs to address. Here's what's left for the Mets to do this offseason following the Skubal signing.

Yes, the Mets still need another starter even after signing Skubal. They have an excellent 1-2-3 punch. The depth behind that top three is not great, however. Here is New York's updated rotation depth chart:

Manaea and Senga both pitched so poorly this past season that they were demoted to the bullpen. They shouldn't be counted on as anything more than emergency options at this point in their careers. Thornton had some moments this summer and Tong is not too far removed from being a top prospect, but yeah, the Mets need another starter. Clearly.

After landing Skubal, I suspect the Mets will aim lower than the second tier of free agent starters (Michael King, Freddy Peralta, Trevor Rogers, etc.) to fill out their rotation. A Clay Holmes reunion would make some sense. Others in that class of veterans make sense too. Think Kevin Gausman, Shota Imanaga, Casey Mize, pitchers like that.

Year 1 post-Pete Alonso at first base went worse than anyone could have expected. Jorge Polanco barely played and was terrible when he did play. Jared Young was fine and owner Steve Cohen isn't running near-record payrolls for fine. Alonso led all first basemen with 5.0 WAR for the Orioles. The Mets finished dead last at the position with -0.8 WAR. Yeesh.

Here are the best available free agent first basemen by FanGraphs projected 2027 WAR:

It ain't great. I think the projections on France, who had an excellent season in 2026, are a bit low, but the fact of the matter is he's only had one year in line with the kind of contract he's likely to sign. Perhaps there's a Luis García Jr. trade to be made with the crosstown rival New York Yankees? García's a clunky fit for the Yankees and might be most useful as a trade chip.

The good news is it won't be hard for the Mets to improve at first base. Getting even an average first baseman would represent an enormous upgrade. Now the Mets just have to go out and find that average (or, preferably, better than average) first baseman and improve their lineup. This might be the single biggest item remaining on their offseason to-do list.

The Mets traded away several relievers at the deadline this summer (A.J. Minter, Brooks Raley, Luke Weaver, etc.), which allowed them to audition a few young pitchers down the stretch. Left-hander Nate Lavender in particular stood out and cemented his place in the 2027 bullpen. The bullpen pecking order currently looks something like this:

Williams was at best inconsistent during his first season with the Mets. Another late-inning reliever to share the high-leverage load (someone to replace Weaver, basically) seems essential. You don't want to pay Skubal all that money only to have the bullpen blow his starts, you know? President of baseball operations David Stearns is adept at building bullpens on the cheap. Spending money is OK too.

Assuming the Mets don't go to the top of the market for Adrian Morejon, the best available free agent relievers are battle-tested veterans like Bryan Abreu, JoJo Romero, and Alex Vesia. Abreu is an excellent buy-low candidate after his rocky first half. There is no such thing as too many good relievers. The Mets should continue adding to their bullpen this winter.

The case can be made that Skubal's contract is only the second smartest contract the Mets gave out this weekend. They agreed to an eight-year, $95 million contract with a ninth-year club option with center fielder A.J. Ewing on Saturday. The deal buys out his six years of team control and two free agent years with an option for a third. That's a nifty piece of business.

I would expect the Mets to pursue extensions with McLean and outfielder Carson Benge next, if they haven't already. McLean and Benge both had terrific first full seasons in the big leagues and look like keepers, like players who can be centerpieces for a World Series contender rather than just tag along for the ride. Locking up McLean and/or Benge would be fantastic work.
